Robert Dallington's Elizabethan English stops partway through chapter XVII, at the word Mustulento — facsimile page 193 of 467. Everything after it has existed in English only under copyright. This is a new translation of the remainder, made from the 1499 Aldine, set beside the Italian it came from so that any sentence can be checked.

271 of 275 pages englished · 88,917 of 90,646 source words (98.1%)

Method. The Italian is the Wikisource transcription of the 1499 Aldine (scanned from the MIT Press facsimile). That transcription is unproofread, so where it looks corrupt we check the facsimile and the 1545 Aldine reprint before translating rather than rendering a scanner error into English. Readings still in doubt are marked [?like this] and explained in the notes; a page is only verified once none remain.

Register. Modern but formal. We do not imitate Dallington — a reader should be able to tell at a glance which English is 1592 and which is ours. The formality comes from vocabulary and sentence shape, not from archaic grammar.

Rights. The 1499 original is public domain, and a faithful transcription of a public-domain work carries no new copyright. Joscelyn Godwin's 1999 translation is in copyright and has not been consulted, quoted, or paraphrased at any point; every English sentence here was made from the Italian in the left-hand column.

Nel proximo latere, vidi de miranda celatura, una Damigella nel aspecto virgineo, matronale maiestate indicante figmento cum summa laude del artifice. De spice coronata, cum elegante defluxo de capigli et habito Nymphale, tenente cum la dextra una farcita copia de maturo grano, et ne l’altra teniva tre stipule cum aristate spice, et agli pedi uno strophiato fasciculo de spice iacente, cum tale subscriptione. Flavae messi. S.

Nel tertio fronte era uno Divo simulachro nudo, cum l’aspecto, cum miro modo et arte expresso, de uno infante coronato de Botryi de uva, tutto de lascivia ridibondo, uno palmite racemato de uva nella leva teniva, et nell’altra una copia completa de uva, fora degli labii cum le fronde et capreoli dependula, a gli pedi del quale stava uno lanigero hirco, cum tale scriptura insculpta. Mustulento autumno.S. L’ultima parte havea una regia imagine de conspicua exscalptura, rubesto nel aspecto et rigido, nella sinistra tenente uno sceptro, mirava verso el coelo, nel aere scuro turbulento et procelloso, et cum l’altra tangente le grandinose nebule. Da drieto similmente l’aere pluvioso et nymbifero. Vestito de pelliceo tegumento sopra el nudo, cum solee antiquarie calciato, et subscripto. Cum tale titulo. Hyemi Aeoliae. S. * *** *

On the next side, I saw, of wondrous carving, a Damsel, virginal in aspect, indicating a matronal majesty in the figment, with the utmost praise of the artificer. Crowned with corn-ears, with an elegant downflow of hair and nymphal habit, holding in the right a stuffed plenty of ripe grain, and in the other holding three stalks with bearded ears, and at the feet a bound little bundle of ears lying, with this subscription:

FLAVAE MESSI · S. — "To the golden harvest. Sacred."

On the third face was a Divine simulacrum, nude, with the aspect — with wondrous manner and art expressed — of an infant crowned with clusters of grapes, all laughing with lasciviousness; a vine-branch clustered with grapes he held in the left, and in the other a full plenty of grapes, out of the lips with the fronds and tendrils pendent; at the feet of which stood a wool-bearing he-goat, with this writing carved:

MUSTULENTO AUTUMNO · S. — "To the must-laden autumn. Sacred."

(— Dallington's translation ends here. What follows is ours.)

The last part had a regal image of conspicuous carving, ruddy in aspect and rigid, holding in the left a sceptre, gazing toward the sky — in the dark, turbulent and stormy air — and with the other touching the hail-clouds. Behind, likewise, the rainy and cloud-bearing air. Clad in a pelt- covering over the nude, shod with antique sandals, and subscribed with this title:

HYEMI AEOLIAE · S. — "To Aeolian winter. Sacred."

Ad questo nobile figmento el praestante artifice, electo solertemente el marmoro havea, che oltra la candidecia sua era venato (al requisito loco) de nigro, ad exprimere el tenebroso aere illumino, et nebuloso cum cadente grandine. Sopra la plana della dicta veneranda, Ara rigidamente rigoroso promineva el rude simulachro del hortulano custode, cum tutti gli sui decenti et propriati insignii. La quale mysteriosa Ara tegeva uno cupulato umbraculo, sopra quatro pali nel solo infixi affirmato et substentato. Gli quali pali diligentemente erano investiti di fructea, et florea frondatura, et el culmo tutto intecto de multiplici fiori, et tra ciascuno palo nel lymbo dell’apertura, o vero hiato del umbraculo affixo pendeva una ardente lampada, et in circuito ornatamente bractee d’oro dalle fresche et verifere aure inconstante vexate, et cum metallei crepituli sonante. Nel quale simulachro, cum maxima religione et prisco rito rurale et pastorale alcune amole, o vero ampulle vitree cum spumante cruore del immolato Asello et cum caldo lacte et scintillante Mero spargendo rumpevano, et cum fructi, fiori, fronde, festa, et gioie libavano, hora drieto a questo glorioso Triumpho, conducevano, cum antiqua et silvatica cerimonia illaqueato el seniculo Iano, de reste et trece intorte di multiplici fiori, cantanti carmini ruralmente Talassii, Hymaenei, et Fescennii, et instrumenti rurestri cum suprema laetitia et gloria, celebremente exultanti, et cum solenni plausi saltanti, et voce foemelle altisone, per la quale cosa non manco piacere et dilecto cum stupore quivi tali solenni riti et celebre feste me invase, che la admiratione de gli praecedenti triumphi. *

For this noble figment the outstanding artificer had shrewdly chosen the marble, which — beyond its whiteness — was veined (in the requisite place) with black, to express the tenebrous, unlit and nebulous air, with falling hail. Upon the flat of the said venerable Altar, rigidly rigorous, stood forth the rude simulacrum of the garden-guardian (Priapus), with all his decent and appropriated insignia. Which mysterious Altar a cupola'd little canopy covered, affirmed and sustained upon four poles fixed in the ground. Which poles were diligently invested with fruited and flowered foliage, and the top all covered with manifold flowers; and between each pole, at the rim of the opening, or gap, of the canopy, hung, fixed, a burning lamp; and, in circuit, ornately, gold foils, by the fresh and spring-bearing breezes inconstantly vexed, and sounding with metallic little rattles.

At which simulacrum, with the utmost religion and ancient rural and pastoral rite, certain little flasks, or glass ampullae, with the foaming gore of the immolated Ass, and with warm milk, and scintillating unmixed Wine, scattering, they broke; and with fruits, flowers, fronds, feast, and jewels they libated. Now, behind this glorious Triumph, they conducted, with antique and sylvan ceremony, the little old Janus ensnared, of ropes and tresses twisted of manifold flowers, singing songs rurally — Talassian, Hymeneal, and Fescennine — and rustic instruments, with supreme joy and glory, celebratedly exulting, and with solemn applause dancing, and female voices high-sounding. For which thing, no less pleasure and delight, with stupor, did such solemn rites and celebrated feasts here invade me, than the admiration of the preceding triumphs.

Then, from here, both of us somewhat progressed, with inexcogitable solace, and proceeding further, I beheld again, at the clear and fresh founts of the gracious and grassy meadows and shady groves, the cascade-Napaeae dancing, and the pleasant Naiads playing, and the marine Nereids singing — clad, some, in the skin of the sea-calf (not harmed by the wrath of supreme Jove), with great bark- vessels of estur in hand stuffed with fruits and flowers, gathered from the gravelly shores, and with diverse solaces idly making festival. Many were, in their hands, bearers of green Thyrses, which at the summit were compacted of orange-flowers, with soft fronds, and of Egyptian roses, yellow and Persian, and of Narcissus-flowers, with handfuls of crimson flowers, and odorous of amuletum; with sylvan Pan the Arcadian, and the demigod sylvan hill-dwellers, and the Dryads, and many others, and Zephyr with his beloved Chloris — to whom he had conceded the power over the beautiful flowers — and many active and singing Shepherds, in their songs expert to contend, and armed with their crooks, praised together, jubilating and applauding, with serious games and jests, with most-ancient instruments of straw and of reed, and with trumpeting Tibiae of bark, of scytala form, of a strange sound, the amorous and omnipotent Jove — festively glorifying — and the holy country-life, and making most-devout the Floralian feasts.

For which thing, how much voluptuous pleasure I felt, I leave to judge to whoever in his cogitation could feign it. Therefore, copiously stuffed with incredible joy, with my most-pleasing companion, traversing, we continued our happy itinerary and amorous walk. Whence, some time, the eyes from their sweet prison and binding — and almost proscription — somewhat removing, Lo! looking above the tender and greenest tops of the wanton trees, I saw a lofty Pterygium (winged pinnacle), above, appearing to me of a round fastigium (gable), esteeming it to be little distant from the whispering shore, toward which she, facetious, was leading me. And in which the gliding and sloping little rivers, that circled the valley, terminated; and from the feet of the most-ornate hills and little mountains — part grassy, part wooded — ran, with most-swift water, in clearest little channels with a grassy and sandy bed, one leaping down to a side. And then again, beyond the said Pinnacle, I saw a superb and eminent cupola, appearing to me covered with livid lead. Which at the summit had a cyma in octagonal form with columns, and above another cupola, and then eight quadrangular piers, covered by a single top, in balustered figure, upon which stood forth a stylus with a most-round Triangle fixed, especially splendent with golden brightness. Whence very pleasingly offered itself to me such a showing, by which I was not —

— mediocrely moved by ardent desire, to behold that more nearly and perfectly, suspecting reasonably there to be a great and antique structure; insomuch that, for this, I almost wished to pray my benign Guide that she conduct me to it — although toward the place we were all the while traversing. But within myself, castigating such desire, I said: "Alas, I dare not obtain that thing for which, with a thorny goad and with sedulous vehement impulse, I am solicited — and especially that thing so warmly desired, which I firmly judge that, obtaining it, I could make myself content above whatever lover. Therefore, repressing and suffocating, and vainly damning such inconsiderate conceit, not demanding henceforth of so long a torment help, with the diurnal pasture of heartfelt sighs — why, then, ought I to ask of this, to me not so opportune (a thing)? Alas, active heart, shared and not wholly mine — how willingly dost thou follow the rapacious hawk of thy living?" — which, wrapping itself in these wanton snares and fecund cogitations, caused, exciting in the inflamed breast, a continual palpitating, as the tear-weeping Pheasant, down from the fronds, impelled to flight by the cruel Falcon, its sad heart beats it.

And so, by these such amorous corollaries frequently agitated, proceeding somewhat beyond our moderate pace, with my Venerable Nymph, eloquently confabulating, and of the marvellous things clearly seen by divine grace affably conferring, with mellifluous eloquence, we arrived finally, a little distant from the re-beaten shore, washed by the pleasant waves of the restless sea. In this place of most-pleasant site, we found, of the building-art, a most-ornate, most-excellently-made and antique temple, of antiquarian workmanship and of the greatest cost, sumptuously skilfully-made, and consecrated to the physizoic (life-giving) Venus.

el circo interstitio secava, ordinò dece archi, residenti sopra columne serpentine, et opposito del substentamento solido, tra uno et l’altro ambiente arco, de latitudine faciale pedi dui, del circulare alamento interiore, resideva promptamente una dolata et expolita columna Corynthia, de celsitudine quanto la Ionica de nove diametri, excepti gli capitelli, de terso Porphyrite, la quale subigeva cum el capitello aeneo, alla trabe recta, circumacta cum el Zophoro et coronice, sopra ducte al solido del fastigio del trabe inflexo, o vero Arco. Gli quali, trabe Phrygio, et coronice, all’ordine del vivo, o vero del firmo della Corinthia, de tanta proiectura eminevano, quanto la linea perpendiculare della praelibata Porphyrica el chiedeva, cum base et capituli de fino metallo causticamente inaurato et perlucido, cum elegante Enthesi, o vero corpulentia. Questo ordine dunque de prominentia regularmente observato era per tutte le Porphyrice aequilibrate et compare. Le quale soprastare al requisito murulo dovevano alla columnatione. Ma el praeclaro Architecto per dare all’area più libera expeditione fece lo intercolumnio pervio. Diqué le trabe inflexe cum gli corni sopra le Ophytice columne terete et tornatile cum frictione illustrabile, residevano, apposito el debito latastro, o vero plintho sopra el capitello per dargli sodo pedamento, et non aereo, per gli operculi insinuati degli dicti capitelli. Et sotto la basi era riservato una semiarula che doveva essere el murulo, sopra le quale semiarule le base de tutte le Ophytice fermamente residevano. Le Corinthie pedavano sopra uno subcolumnio, o veramente uno subbasio di forma de semi Tubulo, de qui et de lì, cum le semi Arule concinnamente colligato. Il quale fue exacto da due quadrature trovate dal diametro della ima crassitudine della Corinthia, restava sexquialtera per el residuo ad undule Thori, Gulule, Nextruli, et Sime, o vero a ssimiglianti liniamenti de sopra et de sotto, conveniente dispensato, decentemente coniugate, cum le base libere sopra deputate. Ciascuno Arco elegantemente del suo cuneo decorato extava, cum puelluli et alternatamente de corticuli cum fogliamento floreo. Et qualunque triangulo specularmente perlustrava uno rotundo diaspreo de colore variato, circinnata egregiamente la sua incasatione, di undiculata fogliatura perlucidamente inaurato.

Nel pillo degli Archi opposito retro alla Corynthia, uno tertio de alveata quadrangula emineva, cum la basi sopra el pavimento extante in facia de un’altra, nel alamento sotto l’arco, che divideva gli fornici infixa, del tutto simigliante. Lo intervallo di queste, da l’una all’altra, gli radii tirati alla circunstantia facevano, sopra la linea degli forinseci Pilli appacte. Sopra gli semicapitelli delle quale ambiva una circumligatione de gratioso operamento. Gli semi Tubuli et hemi Arule erano de luculeo Allabastrite, cum curvescente reste, o vero fasciculi de multiplice fronde et fructi de Lacterii, di Mespili, et Scapi di Papavaro, gravescenti nel suo mediano discenso, di varicante Cymose invinculate sospese et innodate in certi annuli venustamente ornate. Sotto quello circumligamento poco sopra narrato, tra l’una et l’altra striata semiquadrangula nel primario pariete era una quadrangulata fenestra di uno quadrato et semi, come se richiede negli templi antiquarii. La apertione, o vero la luminatione delle quale occupava artificiosamente una speculare, o vero diaphana lamina de petra Sogobrina non temente la vetustate. Diqué in summa octo fenestre erano, perché una parte occupava la porta de esso templo, et per directo del Pronao in fronte un’altra parte della porta cum le valve auree del postico sacello, o veramente del sacro Adyto, la discriptione del quale in altro loco più accommodamente sarà tractata. All’incontro delle sopra recitate columne quadrangule, nel primo murale circuito infixe, gli pilli di fora prominevano, de tanta crassitudine dal muro exacti, quanta quella del muro, ad gli quali la sua latitudine davano le linee degli radii della divisione, dal centro alla circunferentia. La quale latitudine divisa, una portione era per la latitudine del pillastro. L’altra portione ancora in bina partitione deducta, una de qui et de lì l’altra dal Pillo collaterale attribuite, erano per uno arcuare nel solido del muro, o vero concamerato, tra uno et l’altro Pillastro, degli quali Pilli la proiectura, o vero exito, diviso per tertio, usurpava la prominentia del arcuato dal piano del muro scaffato, et gli dui tertii, eminevano gli Pilli, in uno solido muro arcuato et Pilli. Questa exquisita observantia laudavano gli eleganti Architecti, per non dare al muro rude crassitudine tanta, che le fenestre obtuse se accusasseron, cum perspicuo respecto del rude et superfluo solido, et per decoramento exteriore, gli quali arcuati in gyro se involtavano coniugato optimamente l’uno all’altro cum la medesima crassitudine, cum debito illigamento dagli Pilli circunferito sopra el muro per tutto bellamente concincto. Non altramente tra uno et l’altro contrastante arco opportunamente constava.

In the pier of the Arches, opposite, behind the Corinthian, a third of a fluted quadrangular (pilaster) stood forth, with the base upon the pavement, standing in the face of another (in the band under the arch that divided the vaults, fixed) wholly similar. The interval of these, from the one to the other, the radii drawn to the circumstance made, set upon the line of the outermost Piers. Upon the semi- capitals of which went round a circum-ligation of gracious workmanship.

The half-Tubes and half-Altars were of bright Alabaster, with curving ropes, or bundles, of manifold fronds and fruits — of lacterii (spurges), of medlars, and stalks of Poppy, growing heavy in their middle descent, of wavering shoots ensnared, suspended and knotted in certain rings comelily adorned.

Under that circum-ligation a little above narrated, between one and the other striated half-quadrangular (pilaster), in the primary wall was a quadrangular window of one square and a half, as is required in antiquarian temples. The opening, or lighting, of which artfully occupied a mirror-like, or diaphanous, plate of sogobrina stone, not fearing old age. Whence, in sum, eight windows there were — because one part the door of the temple occupied, and, directly opposite the Pronaos in front, another part (the door, with the golden valves, of the rear chapel, or the sacred Adytum, the description of which will, in another place, be more fittingly treated).

Over against the above-recited quadrangular columns, fixed in the first mural circuit, the piers projected outside, worked out from the wall of as much thickness as that of the wall — to which their breadth the lines of the radii of the division, from the centre to the circumference, gave. Which breadth divided: one portion was for the breadth of the pilaster; the other portion, again deduced into a twin partition (one here and one there, the other attributed to the collateral Pier), were for an arching in the solid of the wall, or vaulted, between one pilaster and the other. Of which Piers the projection, or outlet, divided by a third, usurped the prominence of the vault from the plane of the scarped wall; and the two thirds the Piers stood forth, in a solid arched wall-and-Piers. This exquisite observance the elegant Architects praised, so as not to give the wall a rude thickness so great that the windows should accuse themselves obtuse (deep-set), with conspicuous respect of the rude and superfluous solid; and for exterior adornment, which vaults in a ring turned themselves, conjoined most-excellently one to the other with the same thickness, with due binding, from the Piers, carried round upon the wall, throughout beautifully girt. Not otherwise, between one and the other contrasting arch, opportunely it stood.

Notes

All secure; a lucid (if dense) account of a buttressed, thin-walled rotunda.

In questo intervallato vacuo, tra uno et l’altro Pillone, o vero tra le fauce de questi archi prope dicti, sopra el relicto piano murale, excavato era la fenestra. Il quale arcuato tanto quanto egli era distante dal Pillo, tanto circinava sotto la coronice prima extrinseca, ambiente al primo tecto. Dece Pilli, o vero ossi del aedificio erano, et altratanti archi in solido, cum el muro extrinseco, exclusa la facia, ove appacto resideva el sacello. El dicto cornitione amplexando el rotundo sacello, el colligava cum el templo. Oltra questa ligatura ascendeva el suo tecto, che era una caeca cupula dalla maiore per sé distincta et libera. Retorniamo dunque hora allo illigamento interstitio de sopra la circumcolumnatione, o vero Peristylio del Trabe recto, fascia et coronice, porrecto sopra perpendicularemente delle Porphyrice columne, ove nascevano per ciascuna porrectione del illigamento, semicolumnelle de quadratura striate, di egregio Ophytes. Sopra el semicapitello delle quale, ambiva una coronice de liniamento conspicua. Dalla quale el convexo della excelsa cupula, el suo principio sopra incominciava. Infra una semiquadrangula et l’altra de proximo descripte, vidi una proportionata fenestra tempestivamente situata, et de lamina de Bononia de Galia obtusa, constituite in campo deaureato de artificioso Museo. Gli quali spatii cum commensa distributione et aequale partitione, mirai spectatissimamente depicto, de vermiculata tessellatura, la proprietate de ciascuno Mense del anno cum el suo effecto, et de sopra el Zodiaco occurrente cum el Sole operante, et a quello della Luna gli Schematismi, et essa è dita, tra gli menstrui nova cornicula, dividua et praetumida, et el suo circuito, per el quale gli mensi se includeno. Et gli anfracti del Sole indagante, le brume et el solstitio, circuiendo, et della nocte et del giorno la vicissitudine, et la quadrifaria commotione degli tempi, et la natura delle fixe et errante stelle, cum la sua efficacia, suspicai che tale arte fusse quivi ordinata dal nobilissimo mathematico Petosiris, o vero da Necepso. La inspectione delle quale cose, da trahere lo inspectore cum excessivo solacio ad una eximia et miranda speculatione. Non sencia egregio spectaculo, et elegante fictione, et venusta distributione de figure, cum diffinita pictura de coloramento et ombrature, per le quale la commodulatione degli corpi et requisiti lumi, ad complacentia rapraesentantise cum dignissima expressione degli effecti, cum laudabile et iocundo obstento agli sensi del animo. Opera sencia dubio de pensiculatione digna, quanto mai speculare se potesse. Dunque in una divisione el contento del significato delle antedicte operature, de notule antiquarie, elegantemente era inscripto. Gli spatii interpositi tra le semiquadrangule erano circumsepti di fascie, de venusto operamento inscalpte.

In this intervalled void, between one Pillar and the other — or between the jaws of these arches just- said — upon the left mural plane, excavated was the window. Which vault, as much as it was distant from the Pier, so much it circled under the first outer cornice, encompassing the first roof. Ten Piers, or bones, of the building there were, and as many arches in the solid, with the exterior wall — excepting the face where, set fast, resided the chapel (sacello).

The said cornice, embracing the round sacello, joined it with the temple. Beyond this binding ascended its roof, which was a blind cupola, distinct and free of the greater one by itself.

Let us return, then, now, to the interstitial binding above the circum-columnation, or Peristyle — of the straight architrave, fascia and cornice, stretched perpendicularly above the Porphyry columns — where there were born, for each stretch of the binding, little half-columns of quadrature, striated, of egregious Ophite. Upon the semi-capital of which went round a cornice of conspicuous lineament, from which the convex of the lofty cupola began its beginning above.

Between one and the other of the half-quadrangular (pilasters) just described, I saw a proportioned window, timely situated, and of a plate of Bononia (Bologna) of Gaul, opaque, constituted in a field gilt, of artful Mosaic. Which spaces, with commensurate distribution and equal partition, I beheld most- admiredly depicted, of wormwork tessellation: the property of each Month of the year, with its effect; and above, the Zodiac occurring, with the Sun operating; and, to that of the Moon, the phases — and she is called, among the monthly (states), the new little crescent, the halved, and the pre-swollen (full) — and her circuit, by which the months are included. And the windings of the investigating Sun, the solstices and the winter-turns, circling; and of night and of day the vicissitude; and the quadrifarious commotion of the seasons; and the nature of the fixed and wandering stars, with their efficacy. I suspected that such art was here ordained by the most-noble mathematician Petosiris, or by Necepso. The inspection of which things (was) enough to draw the inspector, with excessive solace, to a choice and wondrous speculation — not without egregious spectacle, and elegant fiction, and comely distribution of figures, with defined painting of colouring and shadings, by which the commodulation of the bodies and requisite lights, to complacency representing themselves with most-worthy expression of the effects, with laudable and joyous show to the senses of the soul. A work, without doubt, worthy of pondering, as much as ever one could contemplate. Then, in one division, the content of the meaning of the aforesaid works, of antiquarian letters, was elegantly inscribed. The spaces interposed between the half-quadrangulars were hedged round with bands, carved of comely workmanship.

Notes

Confidence: medium. The completion of the wall (ten piers, ten arches, the round sacello with its own blind cupola joined to the temple), and — the page's real subject — the upper windows glazed with mosaic depicting the twelve Months, the Zodiac, the Sun and Moon's phases, the solstices, and the seasons: a full calendar-astronomy programme in the clerestory, ascribed to the Egyptian astrologers Petosiris and Nechepso. All secure.

Gli reliqui parieti del templo, cum multiplice et variforme de Emblemature, erano operosamente, de pretiosi marmori incrustati, quanto meglio el multiscio Architecto, ad tanta magnificentia de structura imaginando sepe applicare, né forsa tale fue facto ad Ammone. Sopra l’ordine delle Corinthie, de perfectissima scalptura el facondo Apolline resideva lyrante. Et sopra ciascuna delle altre in circuito, sopra conveniente Arule, de tutto integro, una Musa de petra Pilates, ad li opportuni gesti et officio, cum summa laude del Statuario exquisitissimamente scalpte, sopralocate al pretenso dicto de sopra dell’ambiente illigamento. La ingente cupula monstrava maximo inditio, più praesto de divina operatione che de humana obstentatione. Ma se humana, non senza stupore et accusatione dell’ambitione de tanto tentato di arte fusoria dalo ingegno humano, perché considerando tanta vastitate, in una sola et solida conflatura, et iacto de metallo, como io arbitrava, io rimansi summopere mirabondo et allucinato, damnandola quasi alla impossibilitate, niente dimeno questo tale Aerificio, era tutto de Vite nascente fora de bellissimi vasi, della aenea materia, al perpendiculo et ordine stanti della columnatione, diffundendo et gli rami, palmite, o vero surculi, et Capreoli vertiginosamente intricantise, cum gratissimo coniugio, in observantia della formatione del convexo della dicta cupula, la una cum l’altra cum decente densitate, cum foglie, racemi, infantuli scandendo decerpenti, Avicule volitante, Lacerte serpente, ad aemulatione della natura, optimamente exacte, et tuto el residuo pervio. Le descripte operature tanto directamente conducte, che proportionate ne l’area quanto el naturale artificiosamente appariano. De perfectissimo oro tutto collustratamente inaurato. Le apertione, cioè lo intervacuo della fogliatione, fructi, et animali convenientissimamente se praestavano, obturati de crystalline plastre, de diverso coloramento tincte, quale perlustrabile gemme. Alla congruentia della structura opportuna è la integritate dela harmonia, imperoché omni cingibile ligamento intraneo, expostula el concincto extraneo. Gli pili externi continuavano el pedamento Areobato cum gli tre gradi impari, colligante tutto lo imo del tempio, tanto dall’area librato, quanto levato era l’interno pavimento, de sopra agli Areobati, o vero Stylobati, o vero Scabelli, in loco de Base, uno ornato, com Thori, Alvei, Fasce, Gule, et quarti di circulo circumiendo, et ancora d’intorno al sacello concinnamente circinava. Accepto lo infimo suo proiecto dal humano pede, et di sopra gli Pilastri. Gli quali in interstitio erano perterebrati, o vero fistulati, et pertusati, cioè lo imbricio, o vero el compluvio delle aque praecipite, per gli Tubuli fina al solo intromessi, se n

The remaining walls of the temple, with manifold and various-form Emblemature, were laboriously incrusted of precious marbles — as best the much-knowing Architect, imagining, could often apply to so great a magnificence of structure; nor, perhaps, was such made for Ammon. Above the order of the Corinthians, of most-perfect sculpture, the eloquent Apollo resided, lyring. And above each of the others, in circuit, upon a fit Altar, of the whole entire, a Muse of pilates stone — at the opportune gestures and office, with the utmost praise of the Statuary most-exquisitely carved — set above the aforesaid, above, of the encompassing binding.

The huge cupola showed the greatest token, rather of divine operation than of human ostentation. But if human, not without stupor and accusation of the ambition of so much attempted of the founder's-art by human wit — for, considering so great a vastness, in one sole and solid casting and pour of metal (as I judged), I remained most-highly marvelling and hallucinated, damning it almost to impossibility. Nonetheless, this such Bronze-work was all of Vine springing out of most-beautiful vases, of the bronze material, standing at the perpendicular and order of the columnation — diffusing the branches, vine- shoots, or twigs, and Tendrils, dizzily entangling themselves, with most-pleasing conjugation, in observance of the formation of the convex of the said cupola, one with the other with decent density; with leaves, clusters, little infants climbing and plucking, little Birds fluttering, Lizards creeping, in emulation of nature, most-excellently worked out, and all the rest passable (open).

The described works (were) so directly conducted, that, proportioned, in the area they artfully appeared as much as the natural. Of most-perfect gold, all shiningly gilt. The openings — that is, the void of the foliation, fruits, and animals — most-fittingly presented themselves stopped with crystalline plates, of diverse colouring tinged, like translucent gems.

To the congruity of the structure opportune is the integrity of the harmony; for every girdable inner binding demands the outer girdle. The external piers continued the areobate footing, with the three uneven steps, binding all the base of the temple — as much librated from the area as the inner pavement was raised — above the areobates, or stylobates, or Scabelli, in place of a Base: an ornament, with Tori, Alvei, Fasciae, Gulets, and quarter-circles circling round, and again round the sacello becomingly circled. Its lowest projection received (worn) from the human foot; and above, the Pilasters. Which, in the interstice, were pierced through, or tubed, and perforated — that is, the guttering, or compluvium of the precipitate waters, through the Tubes let down to the ground, were —

Notes

Confidence: medium. All secure; the vine-dome is one of the book's supreme architectural inventions.

Lo alamento del primo muro la sua altitudine derivava ad libramento della summitate, della crassitudine degli Trabi inflexi, o vero Archi sopra la columnatione, et quelli del testudinato dal muro a rimpecto della Corinthia columna. Sopra la superficie del quale muro, cioè dello illigamento della circunducta cornitione, era uno canaliolo excavato. Appresso el labro del quale verso el templo se terminava el squammato clivo del aeneo et inaurato tecto. Nel dicto canaleolo sopra el muro nella plana del cornitione excapto, le aque che per piogia per el proclinato tecto scorreano, negli acceptabuli degli Pili infundevanse. — engulfed, of excellent jointing, one conjoined in the tongued (socket) of the other. For in open-air buildings, stairs, compluvium, or gutters, ought not to be placed: first, for the peril of the slip; second, he who makes water next to his own feet destroys, and befouls his footwear. Therefore such inconvenience ought to be fled. The uncovered guttering, by inundating water, excavates the area — and more enormously, if a resistance of subjacent stone opposes — so that the water climbs so much the more to the footing and walls, as it defends itself from the drops, from the resulting drips.

Not without grave injury, damage and loss (and, by the ventilating impetus, the water pours through the walls, rendering them then putrid and earthy, and through the windows leaking, exhausted and vanished every rendering): by the sprinkling of which, there grows in the joints herbage — cotyledon, or cymbalaria, maidenhair, digitello, pellitory, and polypody — and, ready to produce little shrubs and wild figs, a mural ruin, with populous and reviving fibres, or roots, rendering the walls inconstant and rift.

Let us return. The band of the first wall derived its height to the level of the summit, of the thickness of the inflected Architraves, or Arches, above the columnation, and those of the vaulting, from the wall, opposite the Corinthian column. Above the surface of which wall — that is, of the binding of the circum-led cornice — was a little channel excavated. Near the lip of which, toward the temple, terminated the scaled slope of the bronze and gilt roof. The topmost of which summit, above the curved (dome), evenly began, opposite the sublime line of the cornice, of the Frieze and inner Architrave. In the said little channel, above the wall, in the flat of the cornice excavated, the waters that by rain ran down the sloped roof were poured into the receivers of the Piers. And by this way the rivulets of the conceived rain guttered, precipitating to the bottom; and by hidden pipes, or subterranean passages, flowed into the Cistern. Which had a Devourer (overflow-drain), by which the superfluous of the waters went out, and sufficiently for the sacred things remained.

Notes

All secure; Colonna the practical architect.

Per questo modo tra la apertione del muro sotto la cupula, et tra questo adiuncto de Pillastro fundato a llibella sopra lo externo murale circuito, nasceva uno arco hiantemente aperto contrastante, cum liniamento de Trabe. Gli corni del quale pedavano d’ambidui gli lateri del muro et del Pillastro sopra el capitulo d’una semiquadrangula intrusa nel muro, excluso el tertio obvia della intranea de Ophytes et l’altra nel adiuncto del Pillastro. La facia del quale adiuncto de Pillastro dinanti era uno Nicholo, o vero Solio, et inanti questo Solio, o vero Nichio perpendicularmente sopra la piana dil Pillastro era situata per ciascuno una nobilissima statua, cum multiplici acti. Dal latere dextro et sinistro del quale, adiuncto se vedea tale scalptura, quale nel fronte del Pillastro subiecto. L’ultima superficie della crassitudine del arco exteriore ad aequamento era della plana del summo Pillastro. Il lapso dunque dal concincto innitiava, sopra el quale principio usurpava la cupula de fora, et cadeva sopra el Pilo, cum tutto quello liniamento colligantise, che era nel concincto circumacto sotto la cupula, et soto questo lapso resistentia facendo l’arco. Il quale concincto era una coronatione denticulata et echinata, o vero ovolata, cum el suggrundio gyrulato, o vero voragulato cum le pentafilete tra gli verticuli circunducto, cum le occurrente liniature perfecta. Nel plano della superficie de questo illigamento, o vero coronatione lo initio della cupula giaceva, nella proiectura della quale, era uno alveo excavato, nel quale le aque della cupula derivavano discurrendo, et giù per gli alveati lapsi ructuosamente se ingurgitavano negli Pilastri. Supra el lubrico dalla cupula terminando al Pilastro, cioè al suo cimatio, o vero plana, uno cortice, o vero chartella, cooperiendo faceva dui contrarii voluti. Lo uno achosta la cupula supino, et l’altro appresso el Pilo resupino, cum limacale linea facendo gli voluti. Negli inflexi del volume nascevano silique, o vero teche (pregne del suo parto) fabacee, o vero lupinacee. Il quale cortice era intecto de gratiose squamme. Et sopra el convolvulo resupino serpiva cadendo sopra la undiculatione squammea uno folio di Cynara. Il quale volucro cocleale facilmente a norma del circino acconciamente se involve, fermando il stabile et volvendo semicirculo. Of the height treating: it is not completable to have only concluded this universal rule — that a round temple raises itself as much as is its diameter. Then, all the diameter divided into six divisions, four of those rectified will likewise give the last surface of the upper binding.

The rule of the descent of the roof ought not to be neglected: one takes the intercapace from wall to wall, where the ridge-slip ought to be placed, and reduced into two perfect squarings as much as they can come; and, the diagonal extended, cutting the line, discriminating the two squares — thence, beautifully, the slope is exacted.

Finalmente per absolutione di questa mirifica structura di Templo, resta a dire brevemente, che ello era compacto de quadrati de Augustea petra parte, et parte del supranarrato marmoro, in contignatione perfecta sencia ferro et lignatura, cum più subtile investigatione di scalptura, che unque al seculo nostro fare, né imaginare si potesse, né tale ad Api Deo, Sannitico aegyptio construsse. Sotto le base degli Pilastrelli, o vero quadrangule, che era imo et continuo illigamento, nel primo alamento, o vero pariete, et el superiore concincto similmente cum gli capitelli ambiente, ambiva nel aequatissimo pavimento, una lista, o vero fascia de finissimo Porphyrite, quanto era la porrectura del quadrato suo, et contigua quasi sencia disceptatione un’altra de Ophytes. Sotto el suppedio delle columne, era circumacta quanta la sua crassitudine, una lista de Porphyrite, cum due collaterale di durissimo serpentino, cum l’ordine del Peristylio in circumductione. Il simile vedevasi l’orificio della cisterna cincto nel pavimento, una lista de Porphyro et un’altra di Ophytes. Il residuo dil spectatissimo pavimento tra l’orificio puteale et il peristylio, era di mirabile emblemature, di minutali, di tassellulato di fine petre circinantisi elegantemente includevano in partitione deducti, deci rotondi, per diametro pedali. Finally, for the absolution of this marvellous structure of Temple, it remains to say briefly that it was compacted of quadrates of Augustan stone in part, and part of the above-narrated marble, in perfect jointing, without iron and timber, with more subtle investigation of sculpture than ever in our century could be done, nor imagined — nor such did they construct for Apis, the Samnitic-Egyptian God.

Under the bases of the little Pilasters, or quadrangulars — which was the lowest and continuous binding, in the first band, or wall; and the upper girdle likewise, with the encompassing capitals — went round, in the most-even pavement, a strip, or band, of finest Porphyry, as much as was the projection of its square, and contiguous, almost without dispute, another of Ophite. Under the sub-base of the columns was circled, as much as its thickness, a strip of Porphyry, with two collateral of hardest serpentine, with the order of the Peristyle in circumduction. The like was seen of the orifice of the cistern, girt in the pavement — a strip of Porphyry and another of Ophite.

The remainder of the much-admired pavement, between the well-orifice and the peristyle, was of marvellous emblemature, of little-minutiae, of little tessellation of fine stones circling themselves, elegantly included, deduced in partition: ten roundels, a foot in diameter, of their colour and species, the one to the line of the other. There were two of reddening Jasper, most-pleasingly suffused with various spots; two of Litharmenon, of little sparks of gold, more minute, disseminated of rutilant atoms; two of green Jasper, variegated with chalcedonic veins, with reddening and yellow spots; two of Agate, confusedly undulated of milky threads; two, lastly, of most-limpid Chalcedony. And, by the narrowness of the lines toward the cistern, likewise the circular figures decreased.

Under the vaulting were, in the floor, an Asaroton of wormwork emblems — foliage, animals, and flowers, tessellated of most-minute little bodies, of stone-cuttings diligently tessellated, depicted, and most- evenly rubbed smooth, or sculptured. Which art Zenodorus had not, in paving at Pergamon; nor such was the lithostroton at Praeneste, in the shrine of Fortune.

Et alhora incontinente una enucleata admiratione nella calda memoria soccorete, che essendo naturale, che la bianchecia disgregi la potentia visiva, questa cum tanta delectatione, in sé tutto el vedere traheva et congregava, non solamente laedendolo, ma a summo solatio et extremo piacere, quel tanto pretioso obiecto ad sé viscido retinendo ligato, et preso, lo occupava. Onde essendo dalla Sacra Donna le sue divote praecatione agli Dii Forculo et Limentino, et alla Dea Cardinea sinceramente finite, rectantise, la bella Nympha (io solamente cum gli ochii fixi alla sua voluptica operatione persistendo) né per tutto ciò unque mosso me sarei, se non che el subtilissimo panno, le dive delitie tornò a recoprire. Daposcia subitariamente dalla simpulatrice donna el Pesulo amoto, quelle gemelle valve, non strepito stridulo, non fremito grave, ma uno arguto murmure et grato, per el testudinato templo reflectendo exsibilava. Et questo animadvertendo cognovi, per vedere sotto la extrema parte delle ponderose valve de una et de l’altra, uno volubile et terete Cylindrulo, il quale per l’axide nella valva infixo, sopra una tersa et coaequata lastra di durissimo Ophytes invertentise et per la frictione faceano uno acceptissimo tintinare. Oltra de questo ragionevolmente me obstupivi, che le valve ciascuna per se medesima, sencia alcuno impulso se aprisseron. Diqué io mirai uno divo excogitato. Imperoché in quella parte, che una cum l’altra, le valve coivano in la lingulata clausura, dalla interna parte, era una lamina de fino calybe sopra el metallo solidata tersissimo. Erano daposcia mirabilmente due Axule di latitudine triente, di optimo Magnete Indico, al quale lo Adamante non dissideva, di Calistone amatore, agli humani ochii praestabile, dal scordeon mortificabondo. Agli navanti singularmente opportuno, le quale del suo conveniente colore monstravano ceruleo, lisse et illustre, affixe perpollitamente nella crassitudine, dilla apertione dil marmoreo muro, cioè nelle poste, alle ante contigue della artificiosa porta. Dunque per questo modo dalla violentia della rapacitate del Magnete, le lamine calybicie erano violentate, et consequentemente per sé le valve cum temporata lentitudine, se reseravano. Opera excellente et exactissima, non solamente de vedere, ma oltramodo di subtile excogitato. Quanta improbitate di investigato di artifice.

And then, incontinently, an enucleated admiration succoured in the warm memory: that, it being natural that whiteness disgregates (scatters) the visual power, this (whiteness), with so much delectation, drew and congregated all the seeing into itself — not only not harming it, but, to the utmost solace and extreme pleasure, that so precious object, viscidly retaining it bound to itself, and taken, occupied it. Whence, the Sacred Woman's devout prayers to the Gods Forculus and Limentinus, and to the Goddess Cardea, being sincerely finished, and (all) righting themselves, the beautiful Nymph (I alone persisting, with eyes fixed on her voluptuous operation) — nor for all that would I ever have moved myself, had not the most-subtle cloth returned to re-cover the divine delights.

Then, suddenly, by the libation-woman the Bolt removed, those twin valves — not with a strident noise, not a grave rumble, but an acute and grateful murmur, reflecting through the vaulted temple — hissed sweetly. And, animadverting this, I recognised (it), by seeing under the extreme part of the ponderous valves, of the one and the other, a voluble and turned little Cylinder, which, by the axle fixed in the valve, upon a terse and evened plate of hardest Ophite inverting itself, and by the friction, made a most-acceptable tinkling.

Beyond this, reasonably I was stupefied that the valves, each by its very self, without any impulse, opened themselves. Whence, then, all having entered, of a sudden — without looking elsewhere, there affirming myself — wishing to investigate whether the said valves, so timely and moderately, by a counterweight were drawn, or by some other instrument: whence I beheld a divine device. For in that part where, one with the other, the valves met in the tongued closure, from the inner part, was a plate of fine steel soldered upon the metal, most-terse.

There were then, marvellously, two little Axles of a third (foot) in breadth, of best Indian Magnet (to which the Diamond does not dissent — of Callistone the lover, to human eyes outstanding, by the scordeon made mortal (weakened)) — singularly opportune to navigators — which showed, of their fit colour, cerulean, smooth and illustrious, fixed most-polishedly in the thickness of the opening of the marble wall (that is, in the jambs, contiguous to the antae of the artful door). Then, in this manner, by the violence of the rapacity of the Magnet, the steel plates were violated (drawn); and consequently, by themselves, the valves, with temperate slowness, unbolted themselves. An excellent and most-exact work — not only to see, but beyond measure of subtle device. What improbity (audacity) of an artificer's investigation!

In una tabella di Magnete dextrorso del ingresso inscalpto era, di exquisite litere latine antiquarie, quel celebre Virgiliano dicto. Trahit sua quenque voluptas. Nel levorso la tabella vidi di veterrime maiuscule graece elegante inscripto. Παν δει ποιειν κατα την αυτου φυσιν. In latino. A ciascuno fare gli convene secondo la sua natura.

Solevando daposcia gli ochii curiosamente stimulati alla magnificentia di tanto Tempio, et alla vastitate della spectanda et celificata cupula, cum l’altre exactissime parte, de ambitione, et de praestante artificio. De divo excogitato, et de superba operatura, et mirandi liniamenti, de stupenda ostentatione, condito mirabilissimo. Et molto più mirabile iudicai la incredibile bellecia della diva Nympha, la quale illiceva gli ochii mei inspectanti, et tutto l’animo mio teniva. In tanto che dalla recta disquisitione, de qualunque consideranda parte de esso dimovere valesse, et sola essa trahendo coarctasse, a contemplare cum stupore et miraviglia. Dà venia dunque lectore, si omni particula condecente non havesse perscripto.

Et cusì dunque la sacra Antistite intrando el Templo cum la ingenua et praestante Nympha, et io pertinace sequentila, et cum tutte le altre sacre Damicelle, cum le uberrime capillature per gli lactei colli ornatissime cadente, vestite di electissima purpura, et di sopra riportate le tenuissime Gosapine più breve, o veramente curte del primo indumento. Al fatale orificio della mysteriosa cisterna divote et festive ne condusseron.

Nella quale, como dicto fue, altra aqua non intrava. Se non quella che per gli terebrati Pillastri dagli aquarii et compluvii dal fastigato Templo liberamente, senza pernicie della structura, intro se infundevano. La summa sacerdotessa quivi alle virgine fece nuto, et andorono in uno Adyto sacrario, nui tre soli rimasti.

In a tablet of Magnet, to the right of the ingress, was carved, of exquisite antiquarian Latin letters, that celebrated Virgilian saying:

TRAHIT SUA QUEMQUE VOLUPTAS — "Each is drawn by his own pleasure." (Virgil, Eclogue II.65)

On the left, the tablet I saw, of most-ancient Greek majuscules, elegantly inscribed:

ΠΑΝ ΔΕΙ ΠΟΙΕΙΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΗΝ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΦΥΣΙΝ — in Latin, "Each ought to do according to his own nature."

Raising then the eyes, curiously stimulated, to the magnificence of so great a Temple, and to the vastness of the noteworthy and sky-reaching cupola, with the other most-exact parts — of ambition, and of outstanding artifice, of divine device, and of superb workmanship, and wondrous lineaments, of stupendous ostentation, seasoned most-marvellously. La dimonstratione dilla quale Ara succinctamente dicendo, mirai uno conspicuo excogitato di insueta factura. Lo imo dilla dicta sopra il gradato et marmoreo pedamento era uno rotondo latastro. Et similmente nel nascimento dil ambiente foliamento, superassideva un’altra cordicella, et tra questa et un’altra era soppressa una troclea modificatamente alveata, et poscia una coronicetta. Sopra la mensula, overo piano dilla dicta Troclea, superastava un’altra rotonditate regulata, poscia alquanto gululata se contraheva verso la superficie plana et expedita. Nella parte mediana dilla quale promineva uno striato stilo, più porrecto nella inferiore parte sopra la piana cum proportionata crepidine. Diviso dunque il diametro dilla interna rotundatione di questo stilo. Partitione una era alla proiectura ambiente consignata. Il superno capo due portione havea cum tornatile gulule et lo imo ancora debitamente riservatose. Sopradicto stipite tegeva una inversa piana rotundata, tanto in proiecto gyrando, quanto l’extremo exito degli labri dilla subiecta Troclea Ornata nella superiore parte, nello extremo circuito in cliva dimonstratione cum una Sima di spectanda folliatura da una egregia coronetta perpollitamente nascendo. The demonstration of which Altar, succinctly saying, I beheld a conspicuous device of unwonted make. The lowest of the said, upon the stepped and marble footing, was a round little slab. Upon which undulated an auricular foliage, most with polish jagged, and choicely cauliculate, ending its point at a little cord, or knot, or fillet, contained upon the little slab. And likewise, at the birth of the encompassing foliage, sat above another little cord; and between this and another was pressed a trochlea (pulley-moulding) moderately channelled, and then a little cornice. Upon the bracket, or plane, of the said Trochlea, over- stood another regulated rotundity; then, somewhat gulleted, it contracted itself toward the flat and unencumbered surface. In the middle part of which stood forth a striated stylus, more stretched in the lower part, upon the flat, with a proportioned base. The diameter, then, of the inner rotundity of this stylus divided: one partition was consigned to the encompassing projection; the upper head had two portions, with turned gulets, and the lowest also duly reserved.

The aforesaid stalk covered an inverted flat rotundity, turning in projection as much as the extreme outlet of the lips of the subjacent Trochlea, ornated in the upper part, in the extreme circuit, in a sloped demonstration, with a Sima of noteworthy foliage, from an egregious little cornice most-polishedly being born. In the circled content, then, of which little cornice, beautifully occupied the opening of an elegant flower, in balustered lineament fashioned, with the calyxed lips over the flat lambent, and quadripartite into most-pleasant acanthine foliage, gaping. Under which, in the jagged discrepancy, subsided another leaf, artfully carved. Upon the point of which, after the due lineaments, egregiously rounded a knot of exquisite expression. To which, fixed, set, dilatedly stood forth an antiquarian platter of purest gold, with the lips broadish, and a little lacunate (hollowed). In the flat rim of the lips, alternately, stood forth incomparable Diamonds and Carbuncles, with outstanding pyramidal fashioning, in the circuit marvellously disposed, of incredible thickness. Let yield here the Scyphus of most-strong Hercules, the Cantharus of pleasant Bacchus, and the Carchesium dedicated to immortal Jove.

IO NON POSSO UNQUANTULO LASCIarmi suadere, che tali riti, cerimonie, sacrificii, da Numa Pompilio, né a Cerite di Thuscia. Né unque in Hetruria né dal sancto Iudaeo fusseron ritrovati. Né cum tanta religiosa observantia et ordine litavano et adolevano li Memphitici Vati ad Api in Aegypto, nel Nilo la patera aurea immergendo. Né ancora cum tanto religiosissimo venerato in la citate di Rhamnis di Euboia fue culta Ramnusia. Né Iove Anxuro cum tale superstitione fue culto, né quelli che a Faronia afflati tali riti ritrovorono caminando sencia offensione sopra gli carboni accensi. Né tanto tresse furono le edonide clodane, né mymallone di numine aspirate. Quali nel praesente tressero. Meritamente arbitro (oltra questo che palesemente hoe riguardato) per le cose parate, et supersticiosamente disposite succedere dovesse. Imperò che degli capigli la isochrysia Polia Nympha, di cusì facto officio digna negli sacri imbuta et iniciata. Non più presto vide il nuto dilla sacraria monitrice, che dal mundissimo pavimento, sencia voce, indusio, et strepito (niun’altra moventise) promptissima religiosamente se levoe. Onde dalla sacratica monitrice ad una mira urnula hyacinthina da parte collocata nel sacello fue conducta, che di tale artificio mai Mentore non sepe fare. Et io attentissimo riguardantila in tuti acti scrutariamente observava. Et nello aspecto hora la vidi tale, quale il lucidissimo Phoebo cum il novo dì la fresca aurora colorabondo dipinge. Et quivi cerimoniosamente cum le prompte, et intemerate mano, uno odorante liquore fora exhauriva, et il suo lacteo et invermigliato volto spirante purpurante rose, cum le delicate mane madefacte tuto accortamente ella irrigoe. Diqué cusì divotamente purificata cum più sinceritate, quale forsa non hebbe la virgine Aemilia. Dinanti al grado dilla sanctissima Ara, ove extava uno mirando candelabro aureo. Il quale era di exactissimo expresso spectatissimo, et di crasse gemme elegantemente circumornato et glandulato. Nella sua summitate promineva exigentemente una circulata apertione di concula, overo una platina, meno di uno amplexo ulnale. Thimioma et Mastice, ambidui gli Stiraci lo amigdalato Beenzuì il ponderabile Zilaloè blactebisantis, overo ungule indice, et gli felici germini di Arabia. Le quale tute pretiose cose erano cum distributo pondo optimamente gradate. Alle quale la solicita Polia, et cum

I cannot in the least let myself be persuaded that such rites, ceremonies, sacrifices were found out by Numa Pompilius, nor at Caere of Tuscany, nor ever in Etruria, nor by the holy Jew; nor with so much religious observance and order did the Memphitic Seers sacrifice and burn-offerings to Apis in Egypt, immersing the golden patera in the Nile; nor yet with so most-religious a veneration, in the city of Rhamnus of Euboea, was Rhamnusia (Nemesis) worshipped; nor was Jupiter Anxur worshipped with such superstition; nor those who, at Feronia inspired, found such rites — walking without harm upon the kindled coals. Nor so entranced were the Edonian Clodones, nor the Mimallones, aspired by the numen, as in the present they were entranced. Deservedly I judge (beyond that which I have openly beheld) that, by the things prepared and superstitiously disposed, (a marvel) ought to succeed. For, of the hair, the golden Polia Nymph — of such-made office worthy, in the sacred things imbued and initiated — no sooner saw the nod of the sacristan monitress, than, from the most-clean pavement, without voice, delay, or noise (no other one moving), most-promptly, religiously, she rose. Whence, by the sacred monitress, to a wondrous hyacinthine little urn, set apart in the sacello, she was conducted — such as, of such artifice, Mentor never knew to make.

And I, most-attentive, regarding her, in all acts scrutinously observed. And in aspect now I saw her such as the most-lucid Phoebus, with the new day, colouring, paints the fresh aurora. And there, ceremoniously, with prompt and untouched hands, an odorous liquor she drew out; and her milky and vermilioned face, breathing purpling roses, with the delicate moistened hands, all shrewdly, she irrigated. Whence, thus devoutly purified, with more sincerity than perhaps had the virgin Aemilia — before the step of the most-holy Altar, where stood a wondrous golden candelabrum (which was of most-exact and much-admired expression, and elegantly circum-ornated and knobbed with thick gems; in its summit stood forth, exigently, a round opening of a little shell, or a platter, less than an arm's embrace) —

In this, then, was placed the sweetest sperm of the huge whales (ambergris); odoriferous musk; the crystalline and fugitive Camphor; odorous Ladanum of great Crete; Thymiama and Mastic; both the Storaxes; the almond- scented Benzoin; the ponderable Aloewood; blatte-bisantie, or Indian nails (onycha); and the happy germens of Arabia. Which all precious things were, with distributed weight, most-excellently graded. To which the solicitous Polia, and with —

Whence, full and surrounded by marvellous terror, and fearfully agitated, I invoked, silent, whatever divine subsidy and pity. Hora non più praesto che io degustai il miraculoso et suavissimo pomulo, che sencia mora in me sentivi ricentare et rinovare il rude et crasso intellecto, et lo affannoso et moerente core tuto ricrearse in amoroso gaudio delibuto, né più né meno, quale chi nel profundo mare obruto, et fin al fondo immerso cum obstrusi labri, sencia hausto di spirito, di sopra ritorna, le fresche et iucundissime aure avidissimo sumendo se vivifica. Per la quale cosa incontinente in me di ardere più amorose fiamme incomminciorono, et cum più suave cruciato di novelle qualitate d’amore transmutarme mi apparve. Et perciò principiai evidentemente di cognoscere, et effectuosamente di persentire, quale gratie sono le veneree, et di quanta efficacia ad gli terrigeni se praesta et quanto praemio loetamente conseguino, chi per gli delitiosi regni intrepidamente militando, et nelle amorose pugne pervicaci, ad quelli pervengono. Ultimamente dapoi la divota et sacra refectione degli fatali fructi sumpta sencia cunctatione, quel divino germe da gli ochii evanescente disparve. La libante Antistite dil sancto sacello fora ussitene, et Polia pare a llei, et io, et tute.

Cum tale et sì facto ordine terminati et diffiniti gli mystici sacrificii, et libamini et imolatione, et il divino culto, ambedue deposite le sacre veste, et exute, cum eximia veneratione, tuti quegli mysteriosi et pontificali instrumenti, cum domestici et templarii obsequii, nel sacrario riverentemente ripositorno.

Now, no sooner did I taste the miraculous and sweetest little apple, than without delay I felt in me refresh and renew the rude and gross intellect, and the anxious and mourning heart all recreate itself, anointed in amorous joy — neither more nor less than one who, overwhelmed in the deep sea, and to the bottom immersed with shut lips, without draught of breath, from above returns, most-avidly taking the fresh and most-pleasant airs, and vivifies himself. For which thing, incontinently, in me more amorous flames began to burn; and with a more sweet torment of new qualities of love it appeared to me to be transmuted. And therefore I began evidently to know, and effectually to feel, what the Venerean graces are, and of how much efficacy they present themselves to the earth-born, and how great a reward joyously they attain, who — through the delightful realms, intrepidly soldiering, and in the amorous, pertinacious battles — arrive at them. Ultimately, after the devout and sacred refection of the fatal fruits, taken without hesitation, that divine germ (bush), vanishing from the eyes, disappeared. The libant Priestess went out of the holy sacello, and Polia paired with her, and I, and all.

With such and so-made order, terminated and defined the mystic sacrifices, and libations, and immolations, and the divine cult — both, having deposed the sacred vestments, and stripped off, with choice veneration, all those mysterious and pontifical instruments, with domestic and templar obsequies, in the sacristy reverently they re-deposited.

Et quivi trutinatamente la summa Antistite cum praecipua maiestate, cusì familiarmente ne disse. Figlioli mei hora da me expiati, et benedicti al vostro amoroso incepto et viagio andate. Priego ancora la divina matre fausta et affabile se praesti, et ad gli vostri amorosi concepti, intenti, et casi, miserabile, favorevola, et propitia sia. Et nel praesente inclaustrate gli profundi, et crebri sospiri, gli lamentamenti postponete et lassate. Fugate omni moerore. Imperò che già cum la mia instantia questa praesente hora vi sarà salutare et secunda. Dunque a questi mei salubri moniti et proficui imperii l’animo vostro intenda, aciò che essa cum il suo pio et dolce affecto vi concedi foelice successo. Poscia che la sacraria monitrice cum blando affamine hebe dicto. Nui gratie immortale dicendo da tute licentia riverentemente impetrassemo, cum dulcissimi et mutui saluti, indicando il madido volto, che quasi gli molestava il nostro discesso. Tamen valedicendo, fora dil magnifico et superbo tempio uscissimo, et amonita la mia chrysocari Polia dilla via et itinere nostro, finalmente se partissemo. O desiderato cusì diutinamente gratissimo comitato, et foelice, et prospero exito dille transacte tristitie. Hora il mio core afflato d’interna dolcecia, et perfuso di caeleste rore il noxio foco, unquancho non me tituba, ma ferma et evidentemente questa è la mia tanto optatissima Polia. La mia tutelaria dea. Il genio dil mio core. Alla quale benemerente debita gratulatione, io debo di tanto suo famulato alla divina matre, et di tanta ostensione di amore in questo iucundissimo comitato. Queste et simigliante parole summissamente io dicendo, Polia in quel puncto avidutasi dil mio depresso parlare, me riguardoe cum dui festevoli ochii accesi d’amore. Più chiari che lucidissime stelle, sencia la cornuta Cynthia, nel sereno cielo corruscante, non altramente che lo ignito Calybe sopra l’incude malleato scintilla, cusì nel mio percito pecto quelli crebri scintillavano. Et nel parlare venusta cum angelici accenti, cum la purpurante bucca latibulo di omni fragrantia, apotheca di orientale perle, seminario uberrimo di enucleate et dulcicule parolete, tempestivamente mulcendo deliniva omni mia mentale inquietudine. Parlare, sencia dubio, da impiacevolire il terrifico aspecto di Medusa, et di mitigare la atrocitate horrenda dillo infiammato Marte, et dille sue cruentose armature spoliare. Di furare il bellissimo Ganymede dille adoncate granfie dilla suprema alite. Et da teneritudine di scopiare, et minutatamente scindere in parvissime fresule gli durissimi marmori, et cote, et caute, et saxi asperrimi, et abrupti di Persia, et dil invio et nubifero monte Athlante, nella parte di Oceano et acquietando mansuefare, overo cicurire le saevissime fere di Libya, et da vivificare omni pulvereo et cineroso morto, cusì disse. And there, weighingly, the high Priestess, with special majesty, thus familiarly said to us: "My children, now by me expiated and blessed, to your amorous undertaking and voyage go. I pray, again, that the divine mother show herself auspicious and affable, and to your amorous conceits, intents, and cases, be pitiful, favourable, and propitious. And, in the present, encloister the profound and frequent sighs; the lamentings postpone and leave; put to flight every mourning. For already, by my instance, this present hour will be to you salutary and favourable. Then, to these my salubrious admonitions and profitable commands let your soul attend, so that she, with her pious and sweet affect, grant you happy success."

After the sacred monitress with bland speech had said (this), we — immortal thanks saying — from all reverently took leave, with sweetest and mutual salutes, indicating (by) the wet face that our departure almost troubled them. Nonetheless, bidding farewell, out of the magnificent and superb temple we went; and, my chrysocari (golden-graced) Polia admonished of our way and itinerary, finally we departed.

O comitation so long desired, so most-pleasing, and happy, and prosperous exit of the transacted sadnesses! Now my heart, breathed-upon with internal sweetness, and the noxious fire perfused with celestial dew, no longer wavers me — but firmly and evidently this is my so most-desired Polia. My tutelary goddess. The genius of my heart. To whom, well-deserving, due gratulation I owe, of so great her service to the divine mother, and of so great a showing of love in this most-pleasant comitation. These and like words low-voiced saying, Polia, in that instant aware of my depressed speech, regarded me with two festive eyes kindled with love — more clear than most- lucid stars, without the horned Cynthia, in the serene sky coruscating; not otherwise than as the ignited steel upon the anvil, malleated, scintillates, so, in my smitten breast, those (eyes) frequently scintillated. And, in speaking, comely, with angelic accents, with the purpling mouth (hiding-place of every fragrance, apothecary of oriental pearls, most-rich seminary of enucleated and sweet little words), timely, soothing, she delineated (dissolved) all my mental inquietude. A speech, without doubt, to make pleasant the terrific aspect of Medusa, and to mitigate the horrendous atrocity of the inflamed Mars, and to despoil him of his bloody armours; to steal the most-beautiful Ganymede from the hooked talons of the supreme bird; and, from tenderness, to burst and minutely cleave into tiniest fragments the hardest marbles, and whetstones, and crags, and roughest rocks, and abrupt (cliffs) of Persia, and of the pathless and cloudy Mount Atlas in the Ocean-part; and, quieting, to tame, or make gentle, the most-savage beasts of Libya; and to vivify every dusty and ashen dead. Thus she said:

Circa al quale era uno religioso luco. Il quale era sopra aedificato al marisono et lavato litore dal refluo mare. Et quivi ancora restato era una vastitate magna di muri, o vero parieti, et di structure di marmoro albario, et uno fragmentato, et illiso mole di porto apresso. Poliphile dolcissimo mio mira quale digno monumento dille cose magne alla posteritate cusì in tale supinata ruina, et in tanto grumo di rupture di pietre aspero et camelloso relicte. Già nel primaevo fue uno egregio et mirando tempio, circa il quale già solemnissimamente si nundinava, et ingente de mortali multitudine eo omni anno convenivano spectaculi facendo, et per elegante structura, et per gli observati sacrificii diffusamente famoso, molto religiosamente dagli terrigeni celebrato. Which was built up above the sea-sounding and (wave-)washed shore, by the refluent sea. And there, again, was left a great vastness of walls, or partitions, and of structures of white marble, and a fragmented and battered mole of a harbour nearby. In the fractures of which, and left joints, the salt-loving and littoral crithmum (samphire) germinated; and in some places I saw the littoral cakile, and much kali (glasswort), and the odorous marine wormwood; and, by the sandy embankment, eryngo, and purslane, and marine rocket, and very many other celebrated simples — the caratia, and myrsinites, and like shore-dwelling herbs — from which harbour, by many uneven steps, one ascended to the suggestum of the propylaeum of the temple. Which building, by voracious time and by putrid antiquity, and by negligence, to the humid earth collapsed, here and there demolished, had left without capitals the shaft, or decapitated trunk, of some huge columns of Persian stone of red grain; some, with mutual alternation of Mygdonian marble; some had the contracture (fluting) broken — the hypothesis (base), nor the hypotrachelion, nor Astragal was seen; some, again, I beheld of bronze, of marvellous art (such as were not in the Gaditan temple) — but every thing under the open sky, of decay and old age offended.

My frugal and well-mannered Polia here said to me: "Poliphilo my sweetest, behold what worthy monument of the great things, to posterity thus, in such supine ruin, and in so great a heap of stone-breakages, rough and humpy, left. But, because at present abolished is, and ignored, its dignity — thus, as thou seest it lie, disrupted and ruined, expressly destitute — it is denominated the Polyandrion temple. In which, Poliphilo, my little-heart, are many little tomb-pits, where were buried the pulverable bodies of those who, badly, for wicked, unlucky, and lugubrious love, to obscure death, miserable, ceded. In questo loco ad gli celebri ferali et solemni panegyri da diverse regione et provincie contermine et remoti loci parentabondi convenivano, obsecrando et litando il nume di Plutone tricorpo. Alquanto cogita dilla violentia facta a Deianira, et alla pudica Romana, mala et infoelicemente reusita, et di molti altri. Considera che gli omnipotenti dii de gli terreni amori hano resistentia ricevuto, non che homo lacero, et abiectissimo. Revoca nella memoria, che omni longo tempo, a chi pole aspectare accede, et che gli feri leoni ancora per continuati giorni si se cicuriscono, et ciascuno altro silvatico et scaevo animale, et la granifera formica, ancora per assiduo viagio quantunque parvissima in duro silice imprime il suo trito, nonché una diva forma in humanissimo corpusculo latitante, prendere debi in sé vestigio di fervente amore, et cusì observato reprobando confutava tanta noxia, et vexaria passione domante, sperando di conseguire gli amorosi fructi et concupiti effecti et triumphante agonisma. Nella memoria scisitante le sancte oratione, et sacrificii, et libamini, et la extinctione dilla facola. Negli quali divini officii sé, et il suo Poliphilo havea intenta et praecipuamente commemorato cum precature commendaticie, per tanto pensai sofrendo più efficace mercede, et repenso, et lo impetrato conseguire, che cum periculosa improbitate giovare ad gli mei asperrimi languori, et perdere d’indi omni sperancia. La Nympha Polia avidutasi dil versicolore dil mio volto et variare, più che la inclyta Tripolion, overo Teucrion, che tre fiate el dì muta il colore dil suo fiore. "Alas, how wilt thou do here, Poliphilo? Somewhat cogitate of the violence done to Deianira, and to the chaste Roman (Lucretia) — badly and unhappily turned out — and of many others. Consider that the omnipotent gods of earthly loves have received resistance — let alone a lacerated and most-abject man. In memory questioning the holy orations, and sacrifices, and libations, and the extinction of the torch — in which divine offices herself, and her Poliphilo, she had intently and especially commemorated with commendatory entreaties — for so much I thought, by suffering, a more efficacious reward and requital, and the implored (thing) to attain, than that, with perilous improbity, to profit my most-bitter languors, and lose thence every hope.

SOPRA TUTI GLI EXCOGITATI ET exquisiti cruciamenti d’amore non mediocremente obsesso vedendome, et alla praeoptata et salubre, et praesentanea medela, et mia architatrice propinquo essendo obstupefacto mirava che contra omni naturale ordine, quella me più morbidamente inficiava. Et qualunque suo praestante acto, ornato eloquio, morsicante risguardo da sì opportuna salute proximo ritrovantime me abdicavano, onde sempre più multiplicavasi una exhortabile suasione, di volere alla provocante commoditate (grato munusculo ad gli raptori) ingrato non me praestare et pusilanimo. Fremendo come furioso et ringibondo cane, gionta la insecuta fera negli alpestri salti. Cusì io né più né meno furibondo cupitore la propria desiderata praeda quivi gionta, al tuto satisfarmi. Assuefacto hogi mai ad una assidua et familiare morte d’amore, passione per questo non reputava la sua attrocitate, che d’indi ne fusse asseguita. Et peroe omni inconveniente quantunque damnosissimo licito mi suadeva. Diqué la mia eutrapela Polia solerte de l’improbe condictione dil coecuciente Amore, et accortasi per mortificare tanto importuno incendio, et alquanto sincoparlo, et come singulare sospitatrice mia succurrendo cusì benignamente me dice. Poliphile di tuti amantissimo mio già mai non son ignara, che le antiquarie opere ad te summamente piaceno di vedere. Adunche commodamente potes tu in questo intervallo, che nui il signore Cupidine aspetiamo ire licentemente, queste aede deserte, et dalla edace et exoleta vetustate collapse, o per incendio assumpte, o vero da annositate quassate, a tuo solacio mirare, et gli fragmenti nobili rimasti di venerato dignissimi speculare. Et io in questo loco sedendo contenta te aspeteroe, il signore nostro venturo vigile praestolante, che traiectare ne debi al sancto et concupito regno materno. Allhora io grandemente avidissimo, cum l’altre commendatissime opere vise, etiam queste accuratissimo et multivido di contemplare. In quel tempo suavissimo odoranti (sencia altro cogitare absorto) da chosta di Polia per quelli devii aggeri, di fastigiato et vasto cumulo et ruina, in la magiore parte occupate di chamaeciso, et di terrambula et di spini implicita solicito perveni. Above all the excogitated and exquisite torments of love not mediocrely beset seeing myself — and to the pre- chosen and salubrious and present remedy, and my heart-healer, being near — stupefied I marvelled that, against every natural order, she more morbidly infected me. And whatever her outstanding act, ornate eloquence, biting regard, from so opportune a health, finding myself near, abdicated me (drove me off); whence ever more multiplied an exhortable suasion, of wishing, to the provoking commodity (a grateful little gift to ravishers), not to present myself ungrateful and pusillanimous. Fremishing like a furious and snarling dog, the pursued beast having reached, in the alpine leaps: so I, neither more nor less, a furious coveter, the very desired prey here reached, wholly to satisfy myself. Accustomed now to an assiduous and familiar death of love, I did not, for this, repute the atrocity a passion, that thence might be ensued. And therefore every inconvenience, however most-damaging, licit it suaded me. Whence my eutrapela (witty) Polia, shrewd of the improbe condition of blind Love, and aware — to mortify so importunate a burning, and somewhat to syncopate it, and, as my singular preserver, succouring — thus benignly says to me:

"Poliphilo, of all mine most-beloved, I am never unaware that antique works supremely please thee to see. So, conveniently thou canst, in this interval, while we await lord Cupid, go licitly to see these deserted temples, collapsed by devouring and obsolete old age — or by fire assumed, or by many years shaken — to thy solace to behold, and the noble fragments left, of veneration most-worthy, to speculate. And I, in this place sitting, content, will await thee, watchful, awaiting our lord to come, who must ferry us to the holy and coveted maternal realm."

Then I, greatly most-avid — with the other most-commendable works seen — also these, most-accurately and multividuously to contemplate, rose from the happy session, from under the tempered shades of laurel, and of myrtle, and among tallish cypresses (then, about the place, the honeysuckle painting its odorous flowers, where a voluble flowering jasmine, with soft shade, opaquely covered us, disseminating over us copiously its whitest flowers, at that time most-sweetly odorous). In circinatione di questo terreneo overo subterraneo loco, altra operatura non vidi si non appacti sedili dilla propria materia. Tute queste cose cum grande et smisurato piacere, et singular devotione diligentemente mirate di sopra ritornai. Ove mirabondo dilla integritate di questa insigne operatura di ciborio. Tra me confirmai il suspecto, che il cielo dil tempio aperto si fusse. Imperò che la ruina in circuito era aggerata, et questa parte trovai immune. Hora quivi inspectando mossi gli ochii, et vidi una tribuna alquanto integra. Disubito cum gli ochii comitanti gli pedi, ad quella festino andai. Nel cielo dilla quale una artificiosa pictura era ivi rimasta cum incredibile conato et efficientia dill’artifice di opera colorifica di museaco subtilmente expressa. Quivi cavernatamente picto era uno fornice di spissa caligine infuscato monstrante una ingente et trista, et terricula spelunca tuta cariosa quale uno multicavo overo fistuloso pumice. La quale dal lato sinistro verso la mediostima parte vicino ad una asperrima invia, et ferruginea et confragosa rupe terminava. Nella quale se videva uno hiato di concavatura dinanti, et nella facia verso il suo finire distante da uno tofineo saxeo monte scrupeo et chaimeno. Questo per il medesimo modo incavernato all’incontro et pervio. Nella mediata altecia tra l’uno et l’altro traiectava uno bipartito ponte di ferro candente fina al mediato et poscia apparea frigorissimo

— smoke of the sacrifices, ascending, sublimed itself through the passage of the porphyry cupola, and exhaled outside. And, by chance, I suspected that the tholos, or middle summit of the temple, was open, by the Egyptian rite, and (that) of the holy smoke the reek, or burning, without molesting the temple, went out. On the other side of the aforesaid Altar I found, of Roman letters exquisitely excavated, this title (I thought of the altar found by Valesius at Tarentum):

INFERNO PLUTONI TRICORPORI
ET CARAE UXORI PROSERPINAE
TRICIPITIQUE CERBERO

"To infernal Pluto three-bodied, and to his dear wife Proserpina, and to three-headed Cerberus."

In the circling of this earthy, or subterranean, place, other work I saw not, save fixed seats of the proper material. All these things, with great and unmeasured pleasure, and singular devotion, diligently beheld, I returned above; where, marvelling at the integrity of this notable work of the ciborium, within myself I confirmed the suspicion that the heaven (roof) of the temple was open — for the ruin, in circuit, was heaped up, and this part I found immune. Now, there inspecting, I moved the eyes, and saw a tribune somewhat entire. Of a sudden, with the eyes accompanying the feet, to it, hasting, I went. In the heaven (vault) of which an artful painting was there left, with incredible effort and efficiency of the artificer, of colorific work of mosaic subtly expressed.

There, cavern-wise, was painted a vault infuscated of thick gloom, showing a huge and sad, and frightful cavern, all carious, like a many-holed or fistulous pumice; which, on the left side toward the middle part, near a most- rough, pathless, ferruginous and craggy rock, terminated. In which was seen a gap of concavity in front; and in the face, toward its ending, distant from a tufaceous stony mountain, scrupulous and chasmy — this, in the same manner incaverned opposite, and pervious. In the middle height, between the one and the other, passed a bipartite bridge of iron, candent (white-hot) to the middle, and then it appeared most-frigid —
