And within the inner circuit of the most sacred fountain, clear of the join of the sumptuous steps, flowering, purple Adonis sprang up among its kindred leaves, purpling, kept just clear of the water; and on the left side likewise thelygonon flowered with its pale grape-clusters, and on the right arsenogonon — most admirable herbs, and always in flower. And in a circle about the goddess certain small white doves fluttered, dutifully and decorously ministering: dipping their golden bills in the most spotless waters, they mysteriously bedewed the little Cytherean body, and the droplets showed on her translucent flesh as nothing other than orient pearls set there. Close by stood the nymph Peristeria, promptly and even boldly ready, attending with a whole mind upon the services of Venus.

Likewise outside the fountain, upon the stone floor where Peristeria stood, at the right side, three other divine girls stood naked in this manner, inseparably embraced: two of them, Eurydomene and Eurymone, showing their maiden faces toward us; the third, Eurymeduse, turned with her whitest shoulders to us, her hidden hips veiled by the long outpouring of her most golden hair. These were the gracious daughters and handmaids, prompt to the effect of the goddess mother. And she held, lastly, in her divine hands an opened oyster-shell packed with fresh spring roses, and in the other a burning torch.

Now from the topmost step, upon which the columns stood, six little steps more went down to the lip of the fountain, of dark agate; and the flat floor beneath the water was wave-worked with the loveliest and most graceful milky veining, variously spiralling — as delightful an object as could ever be set before the senses. The fountain's water reached to the edge of the fourth step; the others stood clear of it.

And above the upper step there sat at his ease a wanton figure in the shape of a man, the god Nyctelius, whose look was that of a pert and striking girl, most witty, the breast bared by the parting of his garment. His horned head was bound with a vine-band of writhen tendrils, adorned with savoury grape- clusters. He leaned upon two most swift tigers.

By this divine arrangement, then, the most holy majesty of the goddess sat voluptuously in the very middle of the fountain; and the part of the divine body that stood among the waters showed neither more nor less than a ray or splendour of the sun shining through the most polished crystal.

Kneeling there and devoutly persevering, my mind wavered, gazing beyond all measure and to excess, unable to look fixedly upon the divine spirit breathing everywhere. And no less thoughtfully I turned over the cause — by what sweetness of fortune and faith, by what means and merit, such mysteries were granted me to see clearly, and with my eyes unfit for such an object. But I judged it to be only the free will of the immortal gods, and the kind consent and faithful prayer of Polia. Above all things it displeased me that among so many celestial and divine persons I alone stood there contemptible and foreign, in worn and threadbare clothes, unlike them in every way, most abject and most poor; and I would then most gladly have had some means of covering my deformity — as Erichthonius had, to hide his viper feet. And so, stupefied in my mind with incredible wonder, I praised the divine benignity to the utmost, that it had allowed an earth-born man openly to contemplate the works of the gods and the treasure of fermenting nature.

Whereupon the nymphs, perceiving this, with humble and reverent speech obtained leave, and I too, and my lively Polia doing the like, in what manner we then could, having spoken our thanks to the immortal graces, departed. This little history was seen perfectly carved on one long side of the sepulchre; and the son Cupid then gathering the purple blood into an oyster-shell — adding that that divine gore was laid up in that sepulchre, placed with the ash, with every holy rite. Whereupon on the front of our entrance to the sepulchre it was hollowed out in a circle to the size of the square, and then stopped up with the precious stone jacinth, of a transparent vermilion colour, with great coruscation of flaming splendour, burning unsteadily by the light set opposite, so that I could scarcely fix my eyes on it for the wavering.

On the other long side of the sepulchre I saw likewise Adonis, carved with some shepherd-hunters, among some little shrubs, with dogs and the dead boar, and he slain by it; and Venus falling sorrowfully weeping into the pitiful embraces of three half-swooning nymphs, clothed in finest cloth, weeping together with the goddess; and the son, with a little bundle of roses, I saw wiping the maternal eyes, tearful with flowing tears.

There, between the one sex and the other, in a garland of myrtle, I saw thus inscribed: IMPURA SUAVITAS. In like manner on the other little history, in Greek, was thus expressed: ΑΔΩΝΙΑ. So exquisitely feigned in sculpture did all these things present themselves, that I was moved to a sweetness of pity.

In such a case, precipitate and adverse, shall I be able to narrate thee without grave sighs, and dolorous voice, and imperfect, sobbed words — and without irrigation of tears upon the dry cheeks? As the wandering Ulysses, reciting the miserable ruins of Troy to Alcinous, King of the Phaeacians, wept — and (why) does it not break my breast, of cordial sighs, in this most-holy place of felicity, (where such are) denied and interdicted of provocation? And in which place, reasonably, the eyes of tears, and the breast of sighs, sterilise themselves — and, to so blessed and gratifying an audience, remote and alien — and especially in this most-sweet and dearest victory, of my most-appreciated Poliphilo.

Marvel not, then, auspicious, most-comely and heaven-dwelling Nymphs, if I, incontinently — both for my feeble parentage and progeny, and for my first falling-in-love, difficult — some time, sobbing, should interrupt my prolix sermon; worthy, nonetheless, of tarrying, and of a considered and attentive audit. For which unjust and enormous thing, and cruel human impiety — audacious, avaricious, ambitious, superb, and nefarious — the gods (who do not suffer mortal offences unpunished, nor permit any insolence to grow up), irascible that the earth-born should wish, usurping, illicitly to assimilate themselves to the supernal gods — (and to compare with) the most-holy mother of our tremendous lord (to whom now most-deservedly we serve) — showed themselves a raging avenger (not otherwise than Juno to Antigone, and the indignant Eriboea to Isis): the impious temple thunder-blasted, the royal house lightning-struck, reduced to coal, not far distant hence, where by chance she then found herself, remained an eternal name, Casa Carbona; and Murgania (turned) into founts, with all those who in that place found themselves, converted. And so likewise Quintia and Septimia, sisters fleeing not far from Murgania, and they transformed into welling founts. And Alimbrica, made ash, not distant from the said, by the terrific lightnings of the great indigene and lightning-hurling Jove; and all the palace and royal mansion, in that place also built for pleasure, all converted into coals; and the place was called Carbuncularia — thence it leaps forth into a little river. And Astorgia, fugitive, weeping the miserable cases, she too into a little river runs down into her father. And likewise Melmia — their perpetual name they gave to those places, licking in waves, embracing the sweet father Lelio Siliro. And he, transmuted into liquefying matter, augmented by the dear daughters, makes a celebrated river, of most-purged welling waters, which still in that most-pleasant region, flowing, most-fresh is seen: from his truncated name, Sile, it is named. And his consort (Calardia), thunder-struck, weeping the miserable and horrend cases, transmuted herself into a notable fount, from her surname called the fountain Calardia, near the beloved father Tito Butanichio, made into a liquefying river, weeping the hard and cruel lot, mingled with those of his line. And her mother Rhoa, between her husband and her most-beloved brother Caliano, flowing, derive into the sweetest son, Sile.

Nor was any, even of the males, unpunished by the celestial ire and just vengeance. Il quale essendo nella pueritia sua dagli sui cognati signori degli Altinati invitato ad uno solemne anniversario funerale, fora della porta Mania, ove se dinominava ad Manes. Nel quale loco si sepelivano gli cadaveri di tuta la citade, et ancora corrupto il vocabulo riservato, se dice alli Mani. Facti li pomposi obsequii, cum veterrimi riti et more patricio. Rimanse cum alcuni adolescentuli a spasso. Accadete che agli maritimi lochi ritrovantise, apresso la specula, overo phano del porto di Altino nominata Turricella. Dalla quale al presente è vocitato il nobile Oppido Turricello, ivi fundato. In quella sua pubertate dunque dagli invasori Pyrati, furono captivati. Diqué ello fue sorticeamente nella anticha gente Brutia conducto in una famosa citate, che al presente Teramo si chiama. Il quale adoptivato per la ingenua indole sua, da uno nobile et magnifico homo Theodoro, patrizando creve. Et dapò la sufficiente litteratura agli militarii exercitii assiduo strenuamente dava opera. Laonde essendo ad la etate virile pervenuto. Et in progresso di tempo per le cose optimamente geste. Et cum animo forte, excelso generoso, robusto, constantissimamente varie adepte victorie, et tuti gli honori militari perfuncto. Per extinguere cum le eximie virtute il nefasto nome. Per le quale tute cose, dal sanctissimo senato Romano, cum prefectura militare, cum paludamento designato, pervene habitabondo deputato, per adventura, ove esso naque, et ove fue oriundo. Being, then, from this feeble and pitiable case, the only survivor escaped — the first-born Lelio Mauro — who, being in his boyhood invited by his kinsmen, the lords of the Altinates, to a solemn anniversary funeral (outside the Manian gate, where it was named "ad Manes," in which place were buried the cadavers of the whole city, and still, the vocable corrupted, kept, one says "alli Mani"): the pompous obsequies made, with most-ancient rites and patrician custom, he remained with some youths at leisure. It befell that, finding themselves at the maritime places, near the watch-tower, or shrine, of the port of Altino, named Turricella (from which, at present, is called the noble town Turricello, there founded) — in that his puberty, then, by invading Pirates they were captured. Whence he was, by lot, into the ancient Bruttian people conducted, into a famous city, which at present is called Teramo. Who, adopted for his ingenuous character by a noble and magnificent man, Theodoro, grew up patricianly; and, after sufficient learning, to the military exercises, assiduous, strenuously gave heed. Whereupon, being come to the virile age, and, in progress of time, for his things most-excellently done — and, with a soul strong, exalted, generous, robust — most-constantly various victories attained, and all the military honours discharged (like Bellerophon exalted from Heurie): for this reason, no more Lelio Maurio, but, for the egregious condition and outstanding effects, was named Calo Maurio — to extinguish, with the choice virtues, the ill-omened name.

For all which things, from the most-holy Roman Senate, with military prefecture, with the paludamentum (general's cloak) designated, he came, deputed to dwell — by chance — where he was born, and whence he was descended, keeping his fatherland secure and guarded from the barbaric invasions. Which place, of shade and air most-pleasing, and of rivers and founts pleasant, chosen, was named by him Calo Mario — so that, by the benefit of the site, more promptly, amid the molesting assiduity of the infesting foe, he might some time avail to delight himself, where was the verdant area, clad of herbs and of flowers.

There, then, when he was made poliucho (city-protector) — round about, in serviceable memory, and of his dearest mother, an eternal monument — a noble and great city of municipal people (named from the hill Taurisana), and of literal and military study, and of site most-rich and pleasant, and of most-ancient cult, and of sanctity and religion a most-true hostess, upon the hastening and swift Father Sile — and, given it the name of the Pious Mother Trivisia — whence, even to this day, the maternal name it retains (Treviso).

Which, with auspicious increment, a long time, with affluence, with togate peace, and social federations of the neighbours, with life led, pacate, he, happily dominating, possessed; and, of him, the successors —

Ma il vario et inconstante caso, et ordine della fallace fortuna, et infido tempo, sotto a diversi tyranni occupata, finalmente sotto al iustissimo imperio del sancto et feroce Leone Marino, opitulante lo optimo et maximo Iove humanato, essendo felice divenuta Io degli superstiti lineali et prisca familia Lelia, alumna et prognata fui. Et postomi il prestante nome della casta Romana, che per il filio del superbo Tarquino se occise. Nutrita patriciamente, cum molte delitie, perveni al fiore della etate mia. Nel anno della redemptione humana. Dapò gli quatrocento et mille, nel sexagesimo secondo. Io stava come alle vage adolescentule è consueto alla fenestra, overamente al podio del palacio mio, cum gli mei biondissimi capelli, delitie puellare, per le candide spalle dispositi, et dall’ambrosia cervice dependuli, quali fili d’oro rutilanti, alii radii di Phoebo insolando siccantise, gloriabonda accuratissima comente gli pectinava. D’indi a caso passando allhora Poliphilo. Diqué io ardisco di dire, che cusì belli a Perseo non aparveron quegli di Andromeda. Né quegli di Fotide a Lucio. Cusì ello cum intenti et mordaci risguardi accortose, sencia mensuratione et cum incremento d’amore repente se accense. Et il suo tenero et apto core sencia respecto apertosi et per medio ischiantatose (quale ruvido Robure dal fulguratore Iove fulminante percosso, se sfinde) nel primo et puro risguardo. Et Cupido disociato et impigre, cum le sue urente fiamme multiplicabile intromissose, repente sencia alcuna difesa et resistentia succenso et capto. Quale aviculetta simplicula in lacioli imbricosi per poca esca. Et il pisciculo lo hamo inuncando incorre, placidamente cedette. Et del mio legiadro et venusto aspecto desideroso inspectore facto, caldamente appetiva. Il quale molte fiate io nel speculo chiaramente riguardando, dubitava diciò, che quello che ad Narciso advene, a me il simigliante non accadesse. Como nel presente nel mio aspecto patentemente il veddete. Né questo peroe a iactantia debbi esser insimulato. Perché il se adagia. Cusì como fingere et simulare il falso, è vitio. Non meno celare il vero. Dunque de gli novelli et primarii fochi nel pecto suo fundato uno cruciare amoroso, alhora di me affectuoso amante. Diqué già preso in tale amoroso decipulo, per havere qualche condigno consequio di tale Amore. Omni singulo dì, dal palacio mio sedulo viagio prendeva. A l’alte et vacue fenestre riguardando. Non valeva adimpire il frameo desio di rivederme, almeno una fiata. Et per tale cagione havendo cum tanto angore, assai giorni et nocte, passi, vigilie, canti et soni, cum parolette da sospiri formate, cum urgente solicitudine vanamente deperdite. Solamente esso pena et tedio del suo fastidioso et molesto vivere, disperato

— hereditarily, for many years. But the various and inconstant case, and order of fallacious fortune, and infidel time, under diverse tyrants occupied — finally, under the most-just empire of the holy and fierce Marine Lion (Venice), aided by the best and greatest Jove made human — being become happy: I, of the surviving lineal and ancient Lelian family the nursling and progeny, was (born). And, put upon me the outstanding name of the chaste Roman (Lucretia), who, for the son of the proud Tarquin, slew herself — nurtured patricianly, with many delights, I came to the flower of my age, in the year of the human redemption after the four hundred and thousand, in the sixty-second (1462).

I stood, as to the wandering little adolescent-girls is customary, at the window, or the podium, of my palace, with my most-blond hair — girlish delights — over the candid shoulders disposed, and from the ambrosial nape pendent, like gold threads rutilant, at the rays of Phoebus, sunning, drying themselves; glorying, most-accurately, combing (them), I combed them. Heimè Polia Nympha Callitrica. Dia mia. Core mio. Vita mia. Et lanista dolcissima di l’alma mia. Habi pietate di me si nella tua diva natura et nella tua singulare bellecia, vive quella virtute, che l’alma mia, como ad solo nel seculo electo precipuo et primario signore, non renuente, ma festivamente offerentime inclinoe arendevola. Et così più presto me hilaro expono perire, che sencia la tua optatissima dilectione, così miseramente la nocua vita vivi, perché meglio è uno propero interito, che diutinamente morire. Quale più damnosissimo male, et di questo più exitiale unque potrebbe sentire? "Alas, Polia, fair-haired Nymph! My goddess! My heart! My life! And sweetest trainer (lanista) of my soul! Have pity on me — if, in thy divine nature, and in thy singular beauty, lives that virtue to which my soul (as to the sole, chosen, chief and primary lord in the age), not refusing, but festively offering itself, inclined, yielding. Now move thyself, placable, benign, and mitigating, succouring my grave martyrdoms. For I evidently know that, if to those, now, opportunely propitiated, thou succour not, every hope truncated, wholly I see myself perish, for not being able so many my sad pains incessantly to tolerate. And, for a newest refuge of this, at present, to die will be better to me than troublously, and without thy love, to live. And so, rather, I gladly expose myself to perish, than, without thy most-desired affection, so miserably to live the noxious life — because a swift demise is better than to die long. Whence, considering this effect of love, disproportionate to that cause, I cannot, by any pact, come into the cognition of it. For this love appeared to me a sweet thing, but the effect that I feel is supremely bitter. MERITAMENTE POLIA ESSENDO A QUEsto passo divenuta, non poté moderarse, né continerse, che alquanto piatosamente ella non suspirulasse. Et più volte parlando negli amorosi ochi tirate le lachryme, et le rosee guance alquanto fluxe, commosse provocando et similmente le circumastante Nymphe a compassione del doloroso amante Poliphilo, che cusì tristamente egli per vehemente amore, et excessivo dolore fusse perito, trasseno diciò dal profundo del tenero core amorosi suspiri. Et facta uno pauculo di morula, elle solicitavano, che essa il suo gratioso parlare sequitasse. Et interdicti gli caldi sospiri, et affermata la suave voce, cum matronali gesti per questo modo sequendo disse. Beatissime Nymphe, audite grande sevitia, che io non so qual animo mansueto et pio, che hora contra me iniuriabondo non se alterasse. La divina ultione alhora ove era absconsa? che per mia malvasia obstinatione, et dura pervicacia morisse il mio dilecto Poliphilo indignamente. POLIA SOMEWHAT EPILOGUES HER IMMANITY (INHUMANITY); AND (TELLS) THAT, FLEEING, SHE WAS CAUGHT UP BY A WHIRLWIND, AND,
WITHOUT NOTICING, CARRIED INTO A FOREST — WHERE SHE SAW MADE A BUTCHERY OF TWO DAMSELS; TERRIFIED BY THIS, IN THAT
MANNER SHE RETURNED TO HER PLACE. THEN, SLEEPING, THERE APPEARED TO HER TO BE RAVISHED BY TWO EXECUTIONERS. TERRIFIED
THEREBY, MOVING FROM SLEEP, SHE ROUSED THE NURSE AND HERSELF; WHO GAVE HER USEFUL COUNSEL UPON THIS OCCASION.

Deservedly, Polia, being come to this pass, could not moderate herself, nor contain herself, that somewhat piteously she should not sigh. And, more times speaking, the tears drawn into the amorous eyes, and the rosy cheeks somewhat flowing, she commoved, provoking likewise the circumstanding Nymphs to compassion of the dolorous lover Poliphilo — that thus sadly, by vehement love and excessive grief, he should have perished — (and) they drew, from the deep of the tender heart, amorous sighs. And, upon me the placid and humid eyes benignly converting, almost as guilty they damned Polia. But, for so much, being more avid to understand the end of such an unjust occasion, and, a little pause made, they solicited that she should follow her gracious speaking. And there Polia, mannerly, having taken the most-subtle sudary (kerchief) that from the candid shoulders hung, the moist eyes wiped, and the most-purple cheeks dried; and, the warm sighs interdicted, and the sweet voice affirmed, with matronal gestures, in this manner following, said:

"Most-blessed Nymphs, hear a great savagery — that I know not what soul, mild and pious, would not now, against me, injuriously, alter itself. The divine retribution, then, where was it hidden? — that, by my malevolent obstinacy and hard pertinacity, my beloved Poliphilo died unworthily. O celestial vengeance, why wast thou then tardied to delay? — that, rightly, against my iniquitous and perfid soul, in that point, thou oughtest not to have lulled thyself. Nel quale Amore per niuno modo se poteva adherire, né approximarse. Spreta et stupefacta la potentia sua, tanto diversamente ad gli humani cori applicabile signorigiante. "'— most-bitter weeping consecrating. Alas, dolorous and unhappy — in what calamity am I implicated and entangled, in what state I find myself, I avail not to explicate! Who ever saw the subtle fortune with so malign and atrocious an aspect? — that in such a manner (O holy Lady Diana, whom I serve) these my female and virginal flesh must be impiously slaughtered and consumed, and the flower of my pleasant age, in this bushy and sylvestrous grove, perish; and, with so much torment and savagery, the sweet life end?'"

Henceforth I felt the feminine virtues withdrawn, the dear little spirit to flee from its place; and, thence almost removed, at this pass — alas, alas, bitterly weeping, with most-rich rivulets of tears (a peculiar humour, without fail, fecund and ready) irrigating the face, and the breast made-wet — the hands, desperate, in the blond hair I put, with hatred of my adornment, and, the tresses scattered, I wept, and the most-beautiful face, with the hostile nails reddening, I defiled. And, beyond measure tribulating and afflicting myself, this increment to my grave grief accrued: not to be able to exhaust the anguished laments and groans, and, in so afflicting and lost a lot, and in so many tormentable pains, not being able to unseal the cloister of my grief, in the heart impatient more to contain itself. And much more, that there was no mode I might avail to investigate this most-turbulent case — and that, unadvertent, with an innocuous conveyance deported, fearful and trembling, weeping, I found myself unharmed, and, without more hoping, in that same place, whence I was seized and carried off.

O me, heaven-dwelling Nymphs, cogitate how alacritous and content I found myself — let no intellect present itself to explicate — and my mind alienated from the compassionable case (which I held of little (account)) of the wretched Poliphilo, lifeless. Because, from the vexed memory wiped and scraped, in itself it kept him not; but only to the devoured girls, and impiously killed, and most-harshly agonised, held occupied and implicated my mind, and to so most-iniquitous a butchery. Finding no prohibition to the sobbing and frequent sighs, nor an apt mode to settle the anguished mind — with ill difficulty the flowing tears sequestered — at length I returned, no more alive than dead, to the desired and secure mansion, the befallen immanity tacitly re-kindling in the heart, repeatable.

With such similitude, having I all that frightful day in gravest pains consumed, and of sighing weepings all dispensed it — supremely afflicting myself (what fatal cause could it be, that so unwonted and unused, and impious, an immanity, to the ill-fated girls, made, it made me see; and, beyond this, with what sudden mode, from my fleeing journey I was impeded, and through the air reported) — all these things, with solicitous and sighing sobs, straitly considering (alas, afflicted!): O most-happy Nymphs, hear — unless anguish, and weepings, and an ambiguous and dolorous living for the future, a portent to me it were, and a fatal decree, I judged. And, stupefied by this, from stimulating fear I intended, and, by various and turbid cogitations, to conjecture — I could not, by any way, investigate the occult cause. Conscious of this, tacitly, all that unhappy and ill-omened day, groaning, fastidiously consuming it, I passed — in which I would rather have found the pale Corydon (i.e. death) than to have run into so many unvisited sadnesses.

And there, surrounded by acerb dolorations, and copiously by most-molesting pains oppressed, robbed of any security, and not daring, for the nocturnal fallacies, to sleep alone — and, through the dark and ambrosial night, I called to me the dear and revered (in place of a parent) my Nurse, in whom, deposited, reposed, and collocated I had, every my confidence and hope; because, alone, I, in the past, with my chaste Goddess Diana, had been.

Now, both — the hour being arrived that the whitening Cynthia had left the Lamian Rocks and the condense woods, and put an end to the solacing huntings — finally (the bedchamber closed and hedged), we went together to the nocturnal quiescence. And there, the pulsing breast, that still with unquiet beatings frequently beat — scarce, in itself, gathered the frightened and bewildered little spirits, and, with supreme fatigues and efforts, the large course of the round and dripping tears re-shut, somewhat interdicted — I began, badly and with difficulty (frequently, by frightful interruptions, awakened), to sleep.

And, in the deep and first, soporous and soft sleep immersed, the loosened and shattered little body, suffused, slept in the tacit night. Lo, with great and strepent impetus, it seemed to me (as if under the head Eumetes's stone were placed) that the bolts were removed, and the bars seized, and, by breakers-through, the locks broken, and violently laid-open the closed little doors and barred thresholds of my chamber, and to enter —

— I awoke, saying nothing, save, most-sadly sighing, to say: "Alas, alas me! Wah, wah me!" — finding myself all concussed, and full of grave languors. POLIA RACONTA PER QUAL MODO LA SAGACE NUTRICE PER VARII EXEMPLI ET PARADIGMI L’AMONISSE VITARE L’IRA, ET EVADERE LE MINE DELI DEI. ET COMO UNA DONNA DISPERATA PER INTEMPERATO AMORE SEME UCCISE. CONSULTANDO SENZA PIGRITARE IRE ALLA ANTISTA DEL SANCTO TEMPIO DELLA DOMINA VENERE, CHE QUELLO ESSA SOPRA DI CIÒ DEBI FARE. QUELLA BENIGNAMENTE GLI PRESTARAE CONVENEVOLE ET EFFICACE DOCUMENTO.

NON SENCIA SUPREMA FATICA, ET IMpenso labore, Dive et prestabile Nymphe, si pole uno disposito et inclinato animo, ad uno proposito ritrare, maxime per obstinatione difficultato, et per tempo consuefacto, et più dummentre d’indi se ne prehende qualche dilecto spasso et recompensatione. Et quello nel contrario volerlo adaptare et rivertire dil tuto alienato, per fallace estimatione, summamente difficillimo se dimonstra. Et diciò mirando non si presta unoquantulo, si il senso alcuna fiata dipravato, distorto, et corrupto, le cose di materia dulcicule, ingrate, insuave, aspernabile, et amare soleno aparere. Et meno maraveglioso se offerisse. Prestantissime Nymphe, se la candidecia al gli ochii egri, impuri, et lippi, nigriscente aparendo offende. Si le cose rutilante, di livido tectorio, et le micante di candore, et di splendore renitente. Maculate, di rubigine consperse, obtecte di caligine, di vomicione sepiale perfuse, et di atramento infuscate sono damnate, senza dubio, non per diffecto dillo obiecto, ma per il sensuale morbo. Cusì né altramente io. Poscia che alli algori della casta Diana l’animo et la mente mia fermamente essendo habituata et professa, et religata et proscripta, grave peroe et molto difficile rendevase lo ingresso dell’ardente Amore acceptabile. Al quale come a crudele hoste resistere (inexperta della sua dulcitudine) havevame obiectato pertinace contradictorio, et repugnante Nausea. Et volendo dunque probamente intenta, nel gelido core il novello amore inducere, necessitava industriosamente secludere gli repugnabuli contradicenti. Hora la sagace et versuta Nutrice intentissima di volere, quel duro et immassato

"— only, out of so anguished, afflicted, and prodigious a peril, will draw my mind, and the successive life, out of so much mourning and grief."

POLIA RECOUNTS BY WHAT MODE THE SAGACIOUS NURSE, BY VARIOUS EXAMPLES AND PARADIGMS, ADMONISHED HER TO AVOID (THE
GODS') IRE, AND TO EVADE THE THREATS OF THE GODS; AND HOW A WOMAN, DESPERATE FOR INTEMPERATE LOVE, KILLED HERSELF.
COUNSELLING (POLIA), WITHOUT TARRYING, TO GO TO THE PRIESTESS OF THE HOLY TEMPLE OF THE LADY VENUS, (AS TO) WHAT SHE
OUGHT, UPON THIS, TO DO — (WHO) WILL BENIGNLY LEND HER FIT AND EFFICACIOUS INSTRUCTION.

Not without supreme fatigue and expended labour, divine and outstanding Nymphs, can one draw a disposed and inclined soul back from a purpose — most of all (a purpose) made difficult by obstinacy, and by time habituated, and the more while, from it, one takes some delightful diversion and recompense. And to wish to adapt it to the contrary, and revert it wholly alienated (from the former), by a fallacious estimation, most-most-difficult it shows itself. And, marvelling at this, one is not (moved) in the least, if the sense, some time depraved, distorted, and corrupted, is wont to make things of sweet matter appear ungrateful, unsweet, spurnable, and bitter. So, and not otherwise, I: since, to the colds of chaste Diana, my soul and my mind being firmly habituated and professed, and religated and proscribed — grave, then, and much difficult rendered itself the ingress of ardent Love, acceptable.

Into which, after I, with the utmost avidity, had entered — not as was my pristine custom, to the holy Altars religiously to present myself, but, without other saying nor doing, to the place where, scelerate corpse-bearer (Vespillona), I had dragged Poliphilo, I went. And there, with a tearful face, I found him — with the constricted cheeks, truly lying dead, colder and more congealed than a hard marble; and thus he had been, the transacted night, bloodless, wan and pallid — whence, of fear and pity, I paled.

At this pass, most-celebrated Nymphs, bitterly afflicted, mournful and dolorous, the eyes, of tearful miseration, abundantly filled themselves; and torrentially I wept, my low laments syncopating with sounding sighs — desirous, to such a condition, to be consort. And, like the unconsoled Laodamia, moribund, lying-down upon the dead Protesilaus, I prostrated myself, I too, upon the gelid body; and, most-tightly embracing him, I said:

"O most-cruel, terrifying and immature Death — of every good the devourer, and of every sadness the inevitable truncation — lazy not, wish not to delay, at present, to unite me with this one, who, for me (of all the women of the world the most-impious, and, of importunate impudence, malefactress), innocent and guiltless has migrated from this desirable light. This one, who loved me excessively, sole his singular and destined good reputed (me). O me, iniquitous and fierce, beyond every other savagery most-unmild, malign and guilty — more than the most-cruel Phaedra against the innocent Hippolytus. O maledict vital airs — why do you last so little (why not end)? O odious spirit, at present bridled — why findest thou not, now, exit and opening? ... O maledict eyes, that, alive, this one you would not see — you make me, at present, behold him extinct! O tremendous lightnings of high Jove... where remain you extinct — not to incarbuncle me, and, into little dust and ash deservedly, condignly, to reduce (me)?"

And I, as desirous, courteously made it (my heart) only of that worthy and meritorious Lord — an adjunct, and, together, to possess all my life, and my very self, to what he arbitrarily should will. ET PER MANIFESTARE IL SUO URGENTE AFFECTO, GLI DEDE UNO PERSUAVE BASIO PER ARRA DEL SUO EXCESSIVO AMORE. ET QUELLO CHE LA VENERABILE ANTISTA RESPONDE NARRA.

EQUALMENTE IO NON SO CUM QUALE remuneratione Poliphile amantissimo mio. Si non cum sincera fide, et cum verace et ardente amore et cum dolce et eximia pietate alla crudele iniuria illata convenientemente supplendo di ricompensare. Cum aequa vicissitudine, et non cum minore pietate remunerata delle Hyade. Diciò che non meno me commove et provoca la tua honesta petitione, che la praesentia tua per me languescente. Di hora in hora successivamente da quella iudicando sencia fallo compertissimo havendo essere lo effecto. Non altramente crucioso apparendomi che Hectore interempto per la volabile pulvere tracto, cum discorsi grandi di fumido sangue, et cum la flava caesarie cruentata, et cum la facia oblinita et pulverulenta dinanti gli ochii lachrymiferi della dolente et dilectissima Andromeda. O core mio. O solo bene mio. O sperancia dolce, essendose il tuo cruciato et confixo core atristato per mia ferecia di animo interverso, saevo, diro et impietoso, et di errore decepto sì protracto di tempo amaricatose. Trahendo la nogliosa vita in incessabili fleti et pianti. Et nel praesente pieno et stivato nauticamente di tribulosi insulti di amore ad gli mei lachrymabondi ochii rapraesentato. Et di volere sequire la granditate del nobile et digno animo tuo, et di excellentia di amore fervidamente ornato. Il quale hora non troverae sorda et inane audientia. Et diciò in paucula horula vedrai ponere modo, et salubre fine agli tui dolori. Che essendo licente domesticatose uno caeco disio dagli tui edaci ochii del core mio, nel promptissimo pecto, ancora io non me trovo immune né vacua, anti participevola communico cum gli tui mali. Per la quale cosa, non intendo di risparmiare la vita mia che iace nel tuo arbitrio et volere. Et la florida mia et illaesa fanciullecia, agli tui ardenti desiderii, et gratiosi voti deferire. Et non usando già quello che per avanti io ragionevolmente doveva, potria facilmente incorrere nelle inevitabile ire del mio signore Cupidine. Dove

POLIPHILO LAUDA LA PERSEVERANTIA, OBEDIENDO AL IUSSO DEL’ANTISTA. INTERMITTENDO LE PARTE DICTE DEL SUO INAMORARE NARRA ET COME LA VIDDE AD UNA FESTA NEL TEMPIO, OVE D’AMORE SUMMAMENTE EXAGITATO, PIÙ POSCIA SE DOLSE DEL SUO DISCESSO. DIQUÉ LI MANIFESTA IL SUO CRUCIAMENTO PER INVENTIONE DI MANDARLI UNA EPISTOLA.

REVERENDA ET SANCTA ANTISTA, VIRtute è nelle ardue et ferale fatiche, et turbulenti incommodi, et ingrato dispendio, il sapere conservarse, et cum suasibile sperancia, al distemprato animo, freno et temperatura cum probitate et solerte modo ponere, et non impatiente et inconsulto praecipitare et cassitare, ma sufferendo perseverabondo praestarse allo incepto. Quantunque cosa arctissima et difficile se sia et alla volubile et obstinata sorte, et alli sui ludibrii, et insidiosa versutia, cum dissimulamento cedere. Perché non cum fortitudine, ma cum virtute et ingegnio se vince. Quale Bellerophonte perseverante succedette a gloria. Perché a tutti gli stipendii et pretii il strenuo milite la gloria antepone. Volendo dunque io legittimamente lo honorio, che è il debito et expectato premio del mio amoroso Agone consequire. Fermamente valeroso disposime di durare obiecto a che il violentoso Cupidine di me facesse despecta la opprobriosa inconstantia. Arbitrando dementia et levitate essere, il timido et vecorde accedere alla pugna, et niuna cosa praestarse più valida che la fortecia dill’animo. Et non mediocre pudore et verecundia suadentimi al milite advenire, che nel principiato certamine tergavertire et monstrare le spalle. Ma sopra tutto mai al militante se appertiene disperare. Et nella iniciata pugna deficere, perché meglio è non principiare, cha principiato havendo, lassare lo incepto. Diciò si io non vario mi pare che veramente foelice non se pole appellare. Si ello alquanto non hae il suo opposito sustenuto. Perché d’indi nasce insolentia, si genera confidentia, dalle quale procede lo exito infoelice. Quale a Policrate. Et peroe la perfectione del paragonio tanto megliore si sente per il suo contrario, como sopra l’indice Batto chiaramente si comprehende.

Ma per tutto ciò grave non aestimavi per sì facta puella strugerme, né frequentemente morire. Ma ad omni maiore supplicio promptissimo me exponeva festinante. EPISTOLA PRIMA LA QUALE POLIPHILO NARRA ALLA SUA POLIA HAVERE SCRIPTO, ET ESSA UNQUANTULO NON MOVENTISE, LI MANDOE LA SECONDA.

AVIDISSIMO ET SUMMAMENTE PERCUpido di revelare alquantulo la non mediocre fiamma dello impatiente Core. Il quale per il tuo praeclaro et singulare amore assai et validamente infiamato languente se consuma. O di venerato praeclara, et dignissima Nympha, unico in terra di bellecia mirabondo, et perfecto exemplare. Cum queste non parolette, ma profuse et non impedite lachrymule liturando il praesente papyro, ho preso questo tollerabile, et honesto auso, non temerario, ma oltra il credere fortemente impulso dal continuo stimulo, et da molesta assiduitate d’amore infesto, propalare, et dechiarire la mia incredibile passione, et sincera dilectione, che io per te, et ad te porto, mio dolce bene, et dolce mia sperancia, et solo refrigerio de gli mei non cognosciuti affanni, et non pensati da te langori. Alla quale cum pietose voce, et riverente parole, et humile prece, il stato mio in discrimine ricomando, et del mio sagittato et vulnificato core, supplicando soccorso a moderare il disordinato incendio. O Polia diva luce, et mia veneranda Dea, non te insurdire preco hora ad gli mei opportuni mendicabuli, et rogati cum il vulto demisso deprecatore, da calidissimo amore fervescente, te chiamo, te invoco, che festini tempestivamente salubre adiuto, efficace conforto, necessario sublevamento. Il perché essendomi cum gli rapaci uncini degli stelliferi ochii tui il core dal pecto mio divulso, è originata la causa di questo mio inepto et incompto scrivere, da me confuso, et da amore disposito. Et già negli praeteriti giorni, io harei tentato il simigliante, ma unque ritrovare ho potuto modo cusì conveniente et arcano. Dunque per tale rispecto questo mio crucioso tormento manifestare tacitamente restrinxi differendo. Diciò al praesente poscia che non più lento et suspeso, il disiderio mio, intruso, et inclaustrato non l’ò potuto infrenare. Imperoché la violentia del mio amore, cusì vole, et la mia prava sorte, ad questo mio comperto modo, et dulcissimo exordio me urgie, me tira, o Nympha egregia, et di chiunque mai si fusse bellissima. Dunque attendi, et commovite pia, praestate benigna, rendite cum placamento unibile ad tanta benevolentia

(Poliphilo's first letter to Polia:)

"Most-avid, and supremely most-cupidinous, to reveal somewhat the not-mediocre flame of the impatient Heart — which, for thy preclear and singular love, greatly and validly inflamed, languishing, consumes itself — O, of veneration preclear, and most-worthy Nymph, unique in earth of beauty, marvellous and perfect exemplar: with these — not little words, but profuse and unimpeded little tears — blotting the present papyrus, I have taken this tolerable and honest daring (not temerarious, but, beyond belief, strongly impelled by the continual stimulus, and by the molesting assiduity of infest love), to reveal and declare my incredible passion, and sincere affection, which I, for thee, and to thee, bear — my sweet good, and my sweet hope, and sole refrigerium of my unknown afflictions, and, by thee, unthought languors. To whom, with piteous voice, and reverent words, and humble prayer, my estate, in peril, I recommend; and, of my arrow-shot and wound-dealt heart, supplicating succour, to moderate the disordered burning.

"O Polia, divine light, and my venerable Goddess — insurd not thyself, I pray, now, to my opportune mendicables (beggings), and (things) besought, with the face lowered, a deprecator, of most-warm love fervescent; thee I call, thee I invoke — that thou hasten, timely, salubrious aid, efficacious comfort, necessary relief. Wherefore, my heart being, with the rapacious hooks of thy stelliferous eyes, from my breast divulsed (torn), is originated the cause of this my inept and inelegant writing — by me confused, and by love disposed. And, already in the preterite days, I would have attempted the like; but never have I been able to find a mode so convenient and arcane. Then, for such respect, this my tormenting torment, tacitly, I restrained, deferring. For, at present — since no more slow and suspended (was) my desire, intruded and encloistered, I could not bridle it. For the violence of my love thus wills, and my depraved lot, to this my found mode, and sweetest exordium, urges me, draws me — O egregious Nymph, and, of whoever ever was, most-beautiful. Then attend, and commove thyself, pious; present thyself benign; render thyself, with placation, unible, to so much benevolence —"

Se meno fusse l’aspro mio tormento, che la tua usata crudelitate Nympha bellissima et Polia macta virtute alle mie longe afflictione, cum blandivola sperancia mi suaderia a patientia. Ma chiaramente hora io cognosco (per la mia prava et impropitia Stella) la tua cruda saevitia et feritate, qualunque mio incendioso martyrio superchiare et ultra cedere. Dunque che iuva, che vale ad amore di acrescere et incrementare, omni hora, al mio già consumpto corculo, uno tanto dolce foco, si più atroce et frigescente sempre te monstri, più che rigente gelo. Et il pecto tuo più algorifico, che non sono Derce et Nome fonti et più che Salamandra freda che cum il contacto il foco extingue. Alla mia ancillare et servile patientia, et agli mei notificati voti et indicato affecto. Tanto più succenso, quanto più il contrario si oppone della tua ispiacevolecia. Niente dimeno, disvinculare non posso l’amorosa et solida cathena, che sotta tanto molle et premente iugo angariosamente me tene. Immo quanto più ricalcitro, tanto più me implico, preso et captivo in questa amorosa Nassa. Quale muscula nella inextricabile opera di Aragne involuta. Et cusì strictamente revincto, et mancipato et captivo, non valido né apto alla fuga, constrecto son ch’io flectendo me ad te inclini. Perché in te sola consiste la mia libertate pretiosa, et omni mio necessario bene, onde si apertamente intendi Signora mia tanto sincera, et consumata dilectione, et tanta voluntaria subiectione, et tanto activo et operoso amore, perché dunque non voli acceptare tanto liberamente queste cose ad te donate? Cum tutta la vita oblate che nelle tue delicate mano ancipite pende? Heu dulcissima et bellatula Polia soccorri te preco, et lassa et concede penetrare, uno pauculo queste mie (non superbe, non arrogante) ma divote parole nel tuo core. Et suscita in te alquantulo di compassione, recevi gli caldi sospiri, ausculta gli mei domestici et familiari lamenti, cognosci la cordiale benivolentia, attendi ad sì fedele, et mansueto subdito. (Poliphilo's second letter to Polia:)

"If less were my harsh torment than thy accustomed cruelty, most-beautiful Nymph and Polia — a slaughterer of virtue — to my long afflictions, with blandishing hope, it would persuade me to patience. But clearly, now, I recognise (by my depraved and unpropitious Star) thy crude savagery and ferocity, whatever my incendious martyrdom to overcome and beyond surpass. Then, what avails, what boots it, to Love, to increase and increment, every hour, to my already-consumed little heart, so sweet a fire, if ever more atrocious and frigescent thou show thyself, more than rigid ice, and thy breast more frigorific than are Dirce and Nomè, founts, and more than the Salamander, cold, which, with (its) contact, extinguishes the fire? To my ancillary and servile patience, and to my notified vows and indicated affect — so much the more kindled, as the more the contrary opposes itself, of thy displeasingness — nonetheless, I cannot unbind the amorous and solid chain, which, under so soft and pressing a yoke, angariously (oppressively) holds me. Nay, the more I re-kick, so much the more I implicate myself, taken and captive in this amorous fish-trap (Nassa), like a little fly involved in the inextricable work of Arachne (a spider's web). And thus, tightly re-bound, and enslaved and captive, not valid nor apt for flight, constrained am I, that I, bending, incline myself to thee — because in thee alone consists my precious liberty, and my every necessary good.

"Whence, if thou openly understandest, my Lady, so sincere and consummate affection, and so much voluntary subjection, and so active and laborious love — why, then, wilt thou not accept so freely these things given to thee (with all my life offered), which, in thy delicate hands, ambivalent, hangs? Alas, sweetest and beautiful little Polia — succour, I pray thee, and leave and concede to penetrate, a little, these my (not superb, not arrogant) but devout words, into thy heart; and arouse in thee somewhat of compassion; receive the warm sighs; auscult my domestic and familiar laments; recognise the cordial benevolence; attend to so faithful and meek a subject. For, avidly (visibly), I die, I consume myself, of thy immoderate love — insomuch that all the world could not retract me, nor remove me (more firm than Milo), from (this): that I, above every other most-precious thing, excessively love, worship, and revere thee, and that I, bowed, adore thee — O effigied and true simulacrum of a Goddess before my eyes, and to my sight, publicly, so conspicuous and notable represented — in which most-limpidly I see depicted all my health, and expressed all my peace, delight and content."

Modo sperancia mia non denegare a mi, tutto tuo, che cusì pietosamente supplico pietate et al mio urgente foco temperamine, che io senza quello vivere non so, né posso. Et si io potessi non voglio. Il quale sencia dubio, è praecipuo et praeclaro indicio, che il superno Iupiter, cum exquisita et summa diligentia, te hae adfabrefacta, miraculosa ostentatione, di tute excellente bellece depolita. Le quale sencia dubio di tutte le belle damicelle del mondo transcendono praestante, et in te sola complectivamente perfecte. Per la quale cosa unoquantulo non dubito, che ancora quel medesimo Opifice, sì tanto bene, et coelesti doni in te hae fincto, et coelato benignamente della sua similitudine. And, beyond this, with her, infinite times, with the mind I feigned to have a charming colloquy; and, ratiocinating (with her), daringly — intermixed, frequently, the tormentable wailings — I said: 'O my little Nymph, of inhuman and ferine heart — of nature a soft girl (yet) more than solid Steel, and more than murex-stone hardest, more tenacious than a retaining Grapnel, more obstinate than a hinged Beam; more mordant than a rapt Talon, and much more than the cruel and foul Harpies rapacious of my heart: how canst thou persevere in so much hardness and impiety? — more impious than Mithridates, more savage than Alcmaeon, more ungrateful of so much affection than Paris toward Oenone.' — To my prayers, remove, then, these iniquitous abjections from thy Nymphal heart, and this vulgar mark; and assent thyself, propitiated, to my suppliant petitions; concede, my Lady, that I consequute the desired quiet; permit to penetrate thy auditory, my tormentable little sighs; consent to my ardent loves.

And an ardous thing it is to leave that which, some time, in the soul is impressed: enerve, not easily can one. Thence, then, was the exordium and origin, that I, simply ensnared and implicated, in these enveloping nets, and fallacious decoy, and in these subtle, caducous, uncertain, fugacious and momentary snares and sharpnesses of love, enslaved — that, under this molesting Tyranny and condition, and miserable servitude, subjugated and enrolled, I found one sole pleasure and alluring delightment: to love her extremely; nor did I repugn to the flying (arrows) —"

Being, then, in such a manner rapt and sublimated, and, of beholding the celestial works, stupefied — and re-dried the flux of the solicitous tears, and benignly ausculted my miserable laments — the Divine Lady Mother, with an ineffable majesty and sanctimony, and with an unheard and venerable voice, soothing (enough to re-serene the beclouded heavens, to take the noxious armature from Enyalian Mars, and the thunderbolts from the hand of the jaculating Jove, to in-youth the old Saturn, to Ethiopise (darken) the most-beautiful Phoebus, to in-stammer the eloquent Cyllenian (Mercury), and to defile the chaste Diana) — never by the terrestrials heard such (a voice) — proffered divine words, with divine afflation, and with such Harmony, affably, as never, to the empty Syrinx (pipe), the divine lips of the talaric Mercury, (playing) to the eyed Argus, breathed — by the sweetness of which, whatever Cotic whetstone-rock of Libya, nay, whatever Indian Diamond, contaminated and immuted, would have been softened to every softness, tender and fresh.

And, in this manner speaking, she made me secure of my health, and of my prosperous love, and of this my most-jocund postliminium (homecoming), and to thee (Polia) to return. And, with a most-charming little laugh, she said to her offspring: "And thou — if, for the wounded Virgin girl, perhaps to turn-tail from this amorous office, and to relinquish this present soul, thou shouldst fore-attempt — thou shalt be surety (bail)." — "Then, my little body, my lodging: remove from thee all the most-harsh griefs, and every passion, and accept me thus entire into thee, as ever, with thee, conjoined I was — with that most-celebrated name, in me impressed, by which, from thee, I receded; which, otherwise, is carved and impressed, and sealed, within me, vegetable and fecund — (it) was not that of Oenone and of Paris, sculpted in the ramose trees and rugose barks, nor thence ever shall it be erased, nor to be deleted, but eternally consigned, conservable. Now, most-loving host, receive me, thy indigene (native), who, to remedy thy grave and insupportable tribulations, have penetrated and passed through so many waters of weepings, and through so much fire of love, and through so many supreme fatigues; and, finally, up-borne where thy likes cannot be, and have attained so much divine benignity, that I, thence timely sequestered, bear thy most- valiant and most-whole health."

And I, to my re-turned and re-gathered Genius (soul), responded: "Come, indigene inhabitant, and Lady of the supreme citadel of my mind, best rational portion. Come, my heart, domicile of irritable ardour. POLIPHILO DICE, CHE NON PIÙ PRESTO L’ALMA TACENDO, NELLE BRACE DI POLIA VIVO SE RITROVOE. PRECANDO POSCIA L’ANTISTA, CHE PERPETUAMENTE AMBIDUI, GLI DEBI D’AMORE INVINCULARE, POSCIA FECE FINE. ET POLIA CONCLUDE IL SUO NARRARE ALLE NYMPHE, COMO INAMORATA FUE, ET DI ESSA POLIPHILO.

VENERANDA ET SANCTA MATRONA de questo Sacro Tempio Antista praeclara et dignissima. Per aventura incredibile appare, et alieno de fide, che non cusì propere hebbe posto fine l’alma agli sui salutiferi ragionari, in me rigressa la appetibile vita, repente me ritrovai negli stricti et serati amplexi, et succosi et saporosissimi osculamenti de questa Nympha, fiore virgineo redolente. Et cum il servato ordine, il quale essa come lepida, festiva facondamente hae narrato cum miro et amoroso fomento creve intimamente la dilectione nostra fina al praesente caso. Onde essendo hora dinante ad te insigne religiosa et praesidente de questo loco sacro Sancta. Ad te se appertene decentemente de divertire, obliquare, et dimovendo avertire il male, di prosperare il bene, et le humile et ime cose sublimare, le nutante dirigere, et fulcire, le obscure lucificare, et le adverse emendare et corrigere. Dunque fae obsecramo equalmente una indissolubile illaqueatura, et copulando constringe l’animo nostro in uno concorde volere, et in uno desiderio, et confirma et stabilissi il nostro unito et concreto amore, perpetuamente dispositi succumbere et ancillare, servendo al alto Imperio della Divina Matre. Et quivi Poliphilo fece silentio.

La Diva Antista sencia morula inseme ne fece amorosamente consaviare et disse. Cusì como agli Dii immortali hae piasuto non altramente fia. Diqué sancto et iusto a mi pare, che vui dal primo stato doviate ad uno più laudabile demigrare. Siate dunque da me benedicti. Et vivite foelici amorosi, et seduli visitate questo Sancto tempio per vostro tutto confugio et sicuro praesidio del vostro mutuo amore et aequa dilectione. Et quale di vui sarae causa di impedire questo fatale amore, sia persecuto dalle noxie et paurose sagitte et iaculabili teli di Cupidine. Et vulnerato l’uno della d’oro, et l’altro sia infixo della funesta plumbea.

Questo fue dunque il caso et primordio del nostro inamorare, nelle urente fiamme Cupidinee parimente ardendo, Nymphe gloriose, como

POLIPHILO SAYS THAT, NO SOONER (HAD) THE SOUL, FALLING SILENT, (THAN) IN THE ARMS OF POLIA, ALIVE, HE FOUND HIMSELF.
PRAYING THEN THE PRIESTESS THAT, PERPETUALLY, BOTH SHE SHOULD BIND OF LOVE — THEN HE MADE AN END. AND POLIA CONCLUDES
HER NARRATING TO THE NYMPHS, HOW ENAMOURED SHE WAS, AND, OF HER, POLIPHILO.

"Venerable and holy Matron, of this Sacred Temple Priestess preclear and most-worthy: perhaps incredible it appears, and alien of faith, that — no sooner had the soul put an end to its salutiferous reasonings, (than) in me regressed the appetible life, (and) suddenly I found myself in the tight and sealed embraces, and juicy and most-savoury kissings, of this Nymph, virginal flower redolent. And, with the observed order (which she, as charming, festive, eloquently has narrated), with wondrous and amorous fomentation grew, intimately, our affection, up to the present case. Whence, being now before thee, notable religious, and president of this sacred, holy place — to thee it appertains decently to divert, obliquate, and, removing, avert the ill; to prosper the good; and the humble and low things to sublimate; the nodding to direct and prop; the obscure to lucify; and the adverse to emend and correct. Then, we beseech, make equally an indissoluble ensnaring, and, coupling, constrain our soul into one concord will, and into one desire; and confirm and stabilise our united and concrete love — perpetually disposed to succumb and handmaid, serving to the high Empire of the Divine Mother." And there Poliphilo made silence.

The Divine Priestess, without delay, together made us amorously kiss, and said: "As, to the immortal Gods, it has pleased, no otherwise be it. Whence, holy and just to me it seems, that you, from the first state, ought to migrate to a more laudable (one). Be, then, by me, blessed; and live happy, amorous; and, sedulous, visit this Holy temple, for your all refuge and secure presidium of your mutual love and equal affection. And whichever of you shall be cause of impeding this fatal love — be (he/she) persecuted by the noxious and fearful arrows and jaculable darts of Cupid; and wounded, the one, of the golden (arrow), and the other be fixed of the funereal leaden."

"This, then, was the case and primordium of our falling-in-love, in the burning Cupidine flames equally burning, glorious Nymphs — as, perhaps, fastidiously, at length I have narrated." (And, in this saying, Polia — almost weary of the prolix sermoning — made an end.)

All secure; the formal union.

Poscia molto più gratissimo lo intendere del suo alto et nobile origine, et egregia stirpe, et generosa prosapia. I in the least doubt not that the solacing Nymphs — who, for a longish delay, intently had lent benign audience — beyond the supreme delight, took no scanty and exiguous admiration of the loves which Polia, adolescent-girl, distinctly, with such comeliness, narrating, had prosecuted. And, the term imposed to the prolix little history, all rose from the quiet sitting. And, just as she, enucleatedly, with supreme and wondrous fluency, narrated — neither more nor less she bound, inter-weaving the most-odorous florets into a circular little chaplet; and, with the sweet words, it was completed — and, to my head, affectionately genuflecting herself, cunningly she placed (it); and, with twin nectareous and cinnamon lips, dove-wise kissing me. For which thing the Nymphs extremely lauded, approving the most-charming speaking, and the adorned fluency; and that, with elegant procession, and outstanding gestures, and with preclear beauty, had been her most-polished eloquy — high, and of memorable worth. Then, much more most-pleasing, the understanding of her high and noble origin, and egregious stock, and generous lineage, and of the notable family, illustrious and ancient, and of the happy exit of her love, thus orderly recited.

Incontinently, to their Nymphal diversions, jests, and delights, most-facetious and hilarious and all festive, they returned — beginning the muted (many) instruments, with canorous music, to sound, and to the celestial canticles composedly to enter, dancing in a ring around the sacred fount most-limpid, flowing sweet liquors —

Philareta Polia optatissima, et la mia elegantissima Eupathia. Hogi mai excluso omni vulgare pensiculamento, et omni turbido suspecto exploso, tu sei per omni modo quella unica praeelecta tra le mortale, prime primitie amorose della tua illibata, et tutta florea et mundula persona cum eximie lauticie decora Nympha, per la quale flagellosamente affligentime, l’animo mio connexo et connodulato, a tui gratissimi affecti, uno punctulo non è stato quiescente, et sencia gravitate de amaritudine. At present, thou art made more most-pleasing to me than the clear day to the terrestrials, and more opportunely now to me accommodated than the annual harvests to human fomentation.

"Conserve, then, with amorous little custody, my soul in thy eternal Love. POLIPHILO QUIVI FINISSE LA SUA HYPNEROTOMACHIA, DOLENTISE DEL SOMNO CHE NON FUE PIÙ LONGO. ET CHE IL SOLE FUE INVIDIOSO FACENDO GIORNO.

TANTO INOPINABILE DELECTAMENTO surrepto, et dagli ochii mei summoto quel spirito angelico, et subtracto fora dagli somnosi membri il dolce et suave dormire evigilantime, in quel punctulo, Omè Heu me amorosi lectori, tutto indolentime per il forte stringere de quella beata imagine, et foelice praesentia, et veneranda maiestate, lassantime et deserentime tra mira dolcecia, et intensiva amaritudine. Quando dal obtuto mio, se partirono quel iocundissimo somno, et quella diva umbra interrupta et disiecta quella mysteriosa apparitione et sublata. Per le quale fue conducto et elato ad sì alti et sublimi, et penetrabili cogitamenti. Diqué per aventura il Sole de invidia agitato di cusì beato somnio, a depraedare la gloriosa nocte, como publico inimico et Sycophanta della divina Matre, cum gli illuminosi splendori subitoso vene et a dipingere di colore roseo l’albicante Aurora discussa la perpete nocte. Et illustrato et interposito il recentato die, io rimansi stipato et completissimo di dolce, et argutula fallacia. Cogitate dunque quale livore livido, alhora ello harebbe, si io realmente sentisse perfruendo gli proprii et voluptici dilecti, de cusì formosa et diva damicella, et insigne Nympha, che esso non sostene (arbitro perché cum diva non lice) a cconcedermi la longa nocte (da indignatione) di Alcmena. Heu me perché non commutoe egli uno alquantulo della sua celeritudine, cum uno pauculo di secordia, alla mia refecta quiescentia, et praeterire unotantulo il suo statuto? Et perché alhora non mi fue arrogato il Stygio somno della Pyxide della curiosa Psyches? Et quivi Philomela anteluculo flendo promeva, tra gli spinosi rubi operta, et tra boscheti pressi di opaca coma di querculi, involuti della obliquante Periclymeno le violentie dell’adultero et infido Tereo, cum canoro garrito dicendo, Tereus Tereus, eme ebiasato?sospirando emerso et absoluto dal dolce somno repentuscule me lucubrai dicendo. Vale ergo Polia.

Tarvisii cum decorissimis Poliae amore lorulis, distineretur misellus Poliphilus.

.M. CCCC. LXVII. Kalendis Maii.

Poliphilo here ends his Hypnerotomachia, grieving that the sleep was no longer, and that the Sun was envious, and made it day.

So unlooked-for a delight snatched away, that angelic spirit taken from my eyes, and the sweet and gentle sleeping drawn out of my drowsy limbs as I woke — in that instant, alas, ah me, amorous readers, I ached all over from the hard clasping of that blessed image, that happy presence, that venerable majesty, which left me and deserted me between wondrous sweetness and piercing bitterness. When from my gaze there departed that most joyful sleep and that divine shade, the mysterious apparition broken off, scattered, and carried away — by which I had been led and lifted to thoughts so high, so sublime, so piercing.

And then, as it happened, the Sun, stirred to envy by so blessed a dream, coming to plunder the glorious night like a public enemy and an informer against the divine Mother, came suddenly with his shining splendours and painted the whitening Dawn a rosy colour, the long night dispelled. And the new-made day being lit and set between us, I was left crammed and utterly filled with a sweet and subtle deception.

Consider, then, what livid spite he would have had, if I had truly felt, in the enjoying of them, the very voluptuous delights of so shapely and divine a damsel, so matchless a nymph — he who would not endure (because, I judge, with a goddess it is not permitted) to grant me the long night of Alcmena. Ah me, why did he not exchange a little of his swiftness for a little sloth, for the sake of my restored rest, and overrun his appointed hour by just so much? And why was the Stygian sleep out of curious Psyche's box not laid upon me then?

And there Philomela, weeping before daybreak, hidden among thorny brambles and in thickets close with the dark foliage of small oaks wound about with twining honeysuckle, was pouring out the violence of that adulterous and faithless Tereus, saying with tuneful chatter: Tereus, Tereus — [?have I been wronged]. Sighing, risen and released from the sweet sleep, I woke of a sudden into the small hours, saying: Farewell then, Polia.

At Treviso, where wretched Poliphilo was held fast in the most comely little thongs of Polia's love. 1467, on the Kalends of May.

Notes

Confidence: high. The narrative Italian here is unusually plain for Colonna and the classical allusions (Alcmena, Psyche's box, Philomela and Tereus) are all securely identifiable. The one weak point is the corrupt Greek noted below, which is isolated to three words and does not affect the sense of the passage.

  • eme ebiasato? — the transcription reads Tereus Tereus, eme ebiasato?
  • Omè Heu me — the Italian exclamation immediately doubled by the Latin.
  • la longa nocte di Alcmena — Jupiter stopped the sun to lengthen the night
  • Tarvisii — Treviso, where the historical Francesco Colonna's Polia is

The text on this leaf is Latin, not Italian. It is given here in the original with an English rendering beneath, since the Latin is itself quotable and the first three lines carry an acrostic.

F œlix Polia, quæ sepulta vivis
C haro Marte Poliphilus quiescens
I am fecit vigilare te sopitam.

Happy Polia, who being buried yet live: Poliphilo, resting from dear Mars, has now made you, who were lulled asleep, keep watch.

The initials set out from the margin spell F · C · I.

QUI OB LOCI ARITUDINEM, PLUSCULIS POLIPHILI LACHRYMUL[IS] REPULULESCERE NEQUIT.

Traveller, make a little pause, I beg you: here is the perfume-shop of the nymph Polia. And what, you will say, is Polia? That most admired flower, fragrant with every virtue — who, because the ground is parched, cannot put out shoots again for all Poliphilo's little tears. But if you had seen me in flower, you would have seen me surpass all others in beauty, like an exceptional painting; saying, Phoebus, the one you left untouched by your burning, a shadow has felled. Ah, Poliphilo, have done. A flower dried out like this never lives again.

Farewell.
